lessons.title: Learning from Her Mother

activities.prompt: How did Arenla help Sentila learn to shape clay?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Arenla Teaches Sentila
activities.body: Dao was for digging clay. Arenla took Sentila to the riverbank and taught her to use it. She put the right amount in a bamboo cylinder. She turned it into malleable dough, soft enough to shape. She could not hold it. She practised with Arenla for almost a year without learning. Custom sent Sentila to a girls’ dormitory for some nights. Onula supervised the girls and resolved to help Sentila.
keyPoints: Arenla taught Sentila to dig clay with a dao.
Sentila made malleable dough but could not hold it.
Onula resolved to help Sentila at the dormitory.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main events and key words.

activities.prompt: Why does a learner keep practising even when the task still feels hard?
steps: Sentila practised with Arenla for almost a year, because she kept trying to learn.
She still could not hold the lump properly, because the task remained difficult.
Repeated practice alone did not solve the problem, because her skill was still missing.
Therefore, patient help from Arenla and Onula was important alongside repeated practice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Arenla’s Teaching
activities.prompt: Who taught Sentila to dig clay?
options: Arenla
Onula
Sentila
Nobody
activities.explanation: Arenla taught Sentila to dig clay with a dao.

activities.title: Name the Tool
activities.prompt: Arenla taught Sentila to dig clay with a ______.
activities.hint: It was used for digging clay.
activities.explanation: A dao was the tool used for digging clay.

activities.title: Match Each Item
activities.prompt: Match each item with its role in the lesson.
pairs: held the right amount of clay
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a tool, container, material or helper from the lesson.

activities.title: Sentila’s Difficulty
activities.prompt: What stopped Sentila from learning properly?
options: She could not hold dough.
She could remember every step easily.
She could find much more clay.
She had helpful practice at once.
activities.explanation: The lesson says she could not hold the lump of dough properly.

activities.title: Sentila’s Training
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Arenla took Sentila to the riverbank.
Arenla taught Sentila to dig clay with a dao.
Sentila put the right amount of clay into a bamboo cylinder.
Sentila turned the clay into malleable dough.
activities.explanation: This order follows Sentila’s work from digging clay to making dough.

activities.title: Onula’s Decision
activities.prompt: What did Onula resolve to do?
options: Help Sentila.
Leave the dormitory.
Refuse to help.
Stop supervising.
activities.explanation: Onula was a kind widow who supervised the girls. She resolved to help Sentila.

activities.prompt: Why did Arenla take Sentila to the riverbank?
options: To teach Sentila how to dig clay with a dao.
To teach Sentila how to hold a lump of dough.
To show Sentila how Onula supervised the girls.
To show Sentila how clay fit a bamboo cylinder.

why.To teach Sentila how to hold a lump of d: Holding dough was a later problem, not the purpose of the trip.
why.To show Sentila how Onula supervised the: Onula supervised the girls in the dormitory, not at the riverbank.
why.To show Sentila how clay fit a bamboo cy: Sentila used the bamboo cylinder later, when she put clay inside it.

activities.explanation: Arenla used the riverbank to teach Sentila how to dig clay.

activities.prompt: How might Sentila have felt after failing to hold the dough?
options: She may have felt worried about learning.
She may have felt pleased with her progress.
She may have felt bored by the clay.
She may have felt angry with Arenla.

why.She may have felt pleased with her progr: Her difficulty does not suggest pleasure in her progress.
Clay was central to her learning, so boredom is not suggested.
No fact shows that Sentila was angry with Arenla.

activities.explanation: Her repeated difficulty could make her worry about learning.

activities.prompt: In this sentence, what does “malleable” suggest about the dough?
options: It was soft enough to shape by hand.
It was hard enough to keep its own shape.
It was too dry to work with more clay.
It was too wet to hold its shape.

why.It was hard enough to keep its own shape: Malleable dough changes shape instead of keeping its shape.
Clay that was too dry could not become malleable dough.
Dough that was too wet would not hold its own shape.

activities.explanation: Malleable dough can be shaped by hand without breaking.

activities.prompt: What can we learn from Sentila practising for almost a year?
options: She kept trying even though the skill stayed hard.
She stopped trying after her first failure.
She found the task easy very quickly.
She needed no help from other people.

why.She stopped trying after her first failu: Almost a year of practice rules out stopping after one failure.
Her repeated difficulty shows that the task did not become easy.
She practised with Arenla for almost a year.

activities.explanation: Almost a year of practice shows that Sentila kept trying.

activities.prompt: A child calls the dormitory stay a reward. What should we think?
options: It was a custom, not a reward for her clay.
It was a reward for learning how to dig clay.
It was a punishment for holding her dough.
It was Onula’s plan to teach clay.

why.It was a reward for learning how to dig: The story links the stay to custom, not clay practice.
why.It was a punishment for holding her doug: The story does not describe the stay as a punishment.
Onula supervised the girls, but custom sent Sentila there.

activities.explanation: Custom sent Sentila there for some nights.

activities.prompt: What does Onula’s decision to help in every possible way show?
options: She was firmly determined to support Sentila.
She wanted Sentila to leave the dormitory.
She thought practice had made Sentila skilled.
She planned to stop Arenla’s clay teaching.

why.She wanted Sentila to leave the dormitor: No fact suggests that she wanted Sentila to leave.
why.She thought practice had made Sentila sk: Sentila still had trouble, so practice had not made her skilled.
why.She planned to stop Arenla’s clay teachi: Her decision was to help Sentila, not stop teaching her.

activities.explanation: Her decision shows that she was determined to support Sentila.

lessons.title: Onula Gives a New Confidence

activities.prompt: Could watching a friend help someone make something beautiful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A New Chance with Clay
activities.body: Onula noticed that Sentila was very tense. This tension made the clay fail to take the correct shape. Onula promised to teach Sentila how to make a perfect pot. She made a beautiful pot while Sentila watched in amazement. Sentila later created a beautiful pot too. Its mouth was wrong, so Onula advised her to watch Arenla shape it carefully.
keyPoints: Tension made the clay fail to take shape.
Onula promised to teach Sentila.
Onula advised watching Arenla's careful shaping.
activities.explanation: Sentila's tension affects the clay, and Onula offers guidance.

activities.prompt: Why did Sentila's first pot fail, and how did she improve?
steps: Sentila's tension made her clay fail to take its correct shape.
Onula promised to teach Sentila how to make a perfect pot.
Onula demonstrated a beautiful pot, and Sentila later made one successfully.
Watching Arenla's careful mouth shaping helped Sentila gain new confidence.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What made the clay fail to take the correct shape?
options: Sentila's tension
Arenla's slow rhythm
The elongated dough
The pot's wrong mouth
activities.explanation: Sentila was very tense. This made the clay fail to take the correct shape.

activities.prompt: Onula advised Sentila to watch ______ shape the mouth carefully.
activities.hint: This person carefully shaped the mouth while Sentila watched.
activities.explanation: Arenla shaped the mouth carefully while Sentila watched.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the action described.
pairs: pointed out that the pot's mouth was wrong
observed Arenla's left hand and spatula
slackened her rhythm while shaping the mouth
activities.explanation: The lesson connects each person with an action they performed.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order described in the lesson.
items: Sentila successfully created a beautiful pot
Onula pointed out that the mouth was wrong
Onula advised Sentila to watch Arenla
Sentila observed how Arenla held her left hand and the spatula
Arenla slackened her rhythm while shaping the mouth
activities.explanation: The events move from creating the pot to carefully shaping its mouth.

activities.prompt: Why did Onula advise Sentila to watch Arenla?
options: To learn how to shape the mouth
To prepare many pots for drying
To correct Sentila's tense mood
To make a different kind of pot
activities.explanation: Onula advised Sentila to watch Arenla shape the mouth carefully.

activities.prompt: What did Arenla want to do while there were enough sunny days?
options: Make many pots
Watch Sentila make clay
Point out a wrong mouth
Promise to teach Onula
activities.explanation: Arenla wanted to make many pots while sunny days could dry them.

activities.prompt: Onula promised to teach Sentila a perfect pot. She made one first. Why did she do this?
options: To show Sentila the correct method.
To make Sentila feel less important.
To hide how a pot is made.
To test if the clay can be used.

It assumes teaching meant making her feel unimportant.
It assumes the demonstration was meant to hide the method.
It assumes the pot was only a test of clay.

activities.explanation: She wanted to show Sentila how a pot should look.

activities.prompt: Onula showed a beautiful pot, then advised watching Arenla. Sentila made a beautiful pot. What did this show?
options: She could learn by watching careful work.
She could learn only by being shown.
She could make any pot without practice.
She needed another pot to learn.

It mistakes learning by watching for learning only by being shown.
It mistakes one success for making any pot.
It mistakes successful learning for needing another pot.

activities.explanation: Watching careful work helped Sentila make a beautiful pot.

activities.prompt: Arenla held her left hand and spatula. She slowed her rhythm while shaping the mouth. What does this show?
options: She was taking great care with the rim.
She wanted to finish before looking.
She thought the rim did not matter.
She wanted to break the soft dough.

It mistakes slowing down for rushing.
It mistakes care for thinking the rim unimportant.
It mistakes careful work for trying to break dough.

activities.explanation: Her slower rhythm shows care while shaping the rim.

activities.prompt: Arenla wanted to make many pots while sunny days remained. Why did she want these sunny days?
options: To give the pots time to dry.
To make exactly one beautiful pot.
To keep the pots from becoming dry.
To shape each pot's rim more quickly.

It mistakes wanting many pots for wanting only one.
It mistakes sunny days for rainy days.
It mistakes drying for shaping the pot's rim.

activities.explanation: Sunny days help dry the many pots she wants to make.

lessons.title: A New Pot Maker Is Born

activities.prompt: How did Sentila discover her new gift?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sentila Takes Over
activities.body: Arenla completed a batch and asked Sentila to continue. Sentila beat the dough with perfect coordination. Her pot was soon ready. She sped up like a sprinter. She made pot after pot with Arenla's speed and skill. Sentila made only one pot less than her mother. But Arenla was not breathing. Sentila ran for help. Onula sensed something very important. The story announces a new pot maker's birth.
keyPoints: Sentila continued Arenla's work with perfect coordination.
Sentila made only one pot less than her mother.
The story announces a new pot maker's birth.
activities.explanation: Well done. You followed Sentila's sudden new skill.

activities.prompt: A child now makes pots like her mother. How can we tell?
steps: Arenla finishes quickly and asks Sentila to continue, showing trust.
Sentila beats the dough with perfect coordination, showing strong control.
She makes one pot less, showing she nearly matches her mother.
Therefore, a new pot maker has been born.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who did Arenla ask to continue the work?
options: Sentila
Onula
Arenla
activities.explanation: Arenla asked Sentila to continue the work.

activities.prompt: After finding Arenla not breathing, Sentila ran to the village ______ area for help.
activities.hint: Use one word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Sentila ran to the village common area to get help.

activities.prompt: Match each subject with what happened or was believed.
pairs: Were not made by one person alone
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an action or belief from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Arenla completed a batch and asked Sentila to continue.
Sentila began beating the dough.
Sentila realised her pot was ready.
She sped up like a sprinter.
She made pot after pot with Arenla's speed and skill.
activities.explanation: Sentila began, completed a pot, sped up, and made more pots.

activities.prompt: What did Sentila say to her dead mother?
options: She did not want this death.
She wanted many more pots that day.
She asked Arenla to continue the work.
She told Onula to help with pots.
activities.explanation: Sentila did not want her death to happen this way.

activities.prompt: Which sentence best matches the story's ending?
options: A new pot maker is announced.
Arenla returns to make more pots.
Sentila leaves the village for ever.
Onula makes all the pots alone.
activities.explanation: The story ends by announcing the birth of a new pot maker.

activities.prompt: Arenla completes a batch quickly. She asks Sentila to continue. Why?
options: She trusts Sentila to keep making pots well.
She wants Sentila to stop working immediately.
She thinks Sentila cannot learn the work.
She wants another person to finish her work.

why.She wants Sentila to stop working immedi: This mistakes continuing the work for stopping it.
why.She thinks Sentila cannot learn the work: This mistakes an offer of help for doubt about Sentila.
why.She wants another person to finish her w: This assumes Arenla cannot continue, but nothing shows that.

activities.explanation: Asking Sentila to continue shows trust in her skill.

activities.prompt: Sentila beats the dough with perfect coordination. What does this show?
options: She has learned to make pots carelessly.
She must ask Arenla for every single step.
She has learned to make pots with skill.
She thinks every pot should be made slowly.

Perfect coordination does not show careless behaviour.
why.She must ask Arenla for every single ste: Her skill does not show that she needs every step.
why.She thinks every pot should be made slow: Slow work would not explain her perfect coordination.

activities.explanation: Perfect coordination shows that she has learned the skill well.

activities.prompt: Her speed continues after she finds the pot ready. What does this suggest?
options: She has suddenly lost interest in the work.
She must stop because her strength is gone.
She is waiting for Arenla to take over.
She has gained a strong, steady rhythm.

why.She has suddenly lost interest in the wo: Continued speed does not show a sudden loss of interest.
why.She must stop because her strength is go: A sprinter gaining momentum does not mean losing strength.
Continued work shows momentum, not a handover.

activities.explanation: The story compares her continuing speed to a sprinter's momentum.

activities.prompt: Sentila makes only one pot less than Arenla. What does this tell us?
options: Her mother made exactly the same number of pots.
Her skill is close to her mother's level.
Sentila made many more pots than Arenla.
Sentila was too slow to make another pot.

why.Her mother made exactly the same number: One pot fewer is not exactly the same number.
One pot fewer means fewer pots, not many more.
why.Sentila was too slow to make another pot: Her nearly equal output does not show that another pot was too difficult.

activities.explanation: Making one pot fewer shows that she nearly matched her mother.

activities.prompt: Sentila finds Arenla not breathing. She runs for help. How does she feel?
options: She is frightened and needs help quickly.
She is calm because nothing bad happened.
She is angry that Arenla stopped working.
She is proud of the pots she has made.

why.She is calm because nothing bad happened: Her urgent run does not fit a calm response.
why.She is angry that Arenla stopped working: The story shows grief and urgency, not anger about the work.
Pride in the pots does not explain her urgent need for help.

activities.explanation: Finding Arenla not breathing and running for help shows fear and urgency.

activities.prompt: Sentila matches Arenla's speed. Onula senses something momentous. What does she notice?
options: Arenla has lost all skill in the work.
The pot making has suddenly become slower.
Sentila has become a strong new pot maker.
The two women have stopped working together.

A new pot maker does not mean Arenla has lost her skill.
why.The pot making has suddenly become slowe: Sentila's matching speed does not show slower work.
why.The two women have stopped working toget: The announcement shows a new maker, not that the women stopped together.

activities.explanation: Her matching skill and the final announcement show a new maker.

activities.context: Sentila dreamed of becoming a pot maker like her mother and grandmother, although Arenla wanted her to become a weaver. Sentila secretly approached expert potters to learn their skill, but they expected her to lose interest in pottery. She kept her fascination with pot making secret at home and continued watching the potters at work. They mixed the clay with water, pounded it, and pushed their left hands into lumps of softened clay.
activities.prompt: If Arenla again complains that Sentila seems indifferent to weaving, what is the most likely course of action for Sentila?
options: Keep pursuing pottery privately rather than showing a new interest in weaving.
Begin weaving enthusiastically so Arenla stops complaining.
Tell Arenla that weaving is now Sentila's main interest.
Stop approaching the potters and accept weaving as her only future.

why.Begin weaving enthusiastically so Arenla: Her fascination had not ended, so this does not fit her behaviour.
why.Tell Arenla that weaving is now Sentila': Her real ambition was pot making, not weaving.
why.Stop approaching the potters and accept: She kept watching and learning from the potters.

activities.explanation: Her interest remains private, while she continues learning pottery.

activities.context: Sentila dreamed of becoming a pot maker like her mother and grandmother, although Arenla wanted her to become a weaver. Sentila secretly approached expert potters to learn their skill, but they expected her to lose interest in pottery. She kept her fascination with pot making secret at home and continued watching the potters at work. They mixed the clay with water, pounded it, and pushed their left hands into lumps of softened clay.
activities.prompt: What should a learner do first to prepare the clay for the left-hand shaping step?
options: Combine the clay with water and pound it before working it into softened lumps.
Push left hands into the lumps before combining clay with water.
Pound the clay only after pressing left hands into softened lumps.
Mix water into the clay after completing the left-hand shaping step.

why.Push left hands into the lumps before co: The clay was mixed and pounded before the left-hand step.
why.Pound the clay only after pressing left: The case places pounding before the shaping step.
why.Mix water into the clay after completing: The case places mixing with water before the shaping step.

activities.explanation: This follows the order shown in the case.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Sentila kept her fascination with pot making secret at home.
Reason (R): She wanted to learn pottery from expert potters.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both are true, and learning from expert potters explains why she kept her interest private.

activities.prompt: Explain why Sentila's dream and the way she pursued it were different from Arenla's hope for her.
activities.answer: Sentila's dream was to follow the pot-making tradition of her mother and grandmother. Arenla, however, wanted her to become a weaver, so she regarded Sentila's indifference to weaving as a problem. Rather than openly disagreeing with Arenla, Sentila kept her fascination with pot making secret at home. She secretly approached expert potters and continued watching them work. Her actions showed that her interest was serious and hidden, while Arenla's hope concerned the craft Sentila was being encouraged to learn.
points: Sentila dreamed of becoming a pot maker.
Arenla wanted Sentila to become a weaver.
Sentila kept her interest secret at home.
She secretly learned from expert potters.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The riverbank clay was sixteen kilometres from the village, and reaching it meant climbing down a steep drop. Arenla carried heavy loads uphill, so her back ached. Pounding the clay in bamboo cylinders was tiring, and she often dropped the mould when exhausted. A batch of pots took several months to finish, but she received only a few rupees. Learning weaving could earn more and provide cloth for the family.
activities.prompt: If Arenla chooses weaving instead of spending several months making a batch of pots, what benefit will she gain?
options: She will be able to work indoors in every season.
She will have to return to the riverbank in every season.
Making a shawl will take more time than making a batch of pots.
Her family will receive no cloth from her weaving.

why.She will have to return to the riverbank: Indoor weaving does not require visits to the riverbank.
why.Making a shawl will take more time than: One shawl takes less time than a batch of pots.
why.Her family will receive no cloth from he: Weaving can provide cloth for the family.

activities.explanation: Weaving can be done indoors in every season.

activities.context: The riverbank clay was sixteen kilometres from the village, and reaching it meant climbing down a steep drop. Arenla carried heavy loads uphill, so her back ached. Pounding the clay in bamboo cylinders was tiring, and she often dropped the mould when exhausted. A batch of pots took several months to finish, but she received only a few rupees. Learning weaving could earn more and provide cloth for the family.
activities.prompt: If Arenla carried lighter loads uphill from the riverbank, what would most likely happen?
options: Her back would be less likely to ache.
She would never feel tired from making the pots.
A batch of pots would be completed in a few hours.
She would receive more rupees for the same batch.

why.She would never feel tired from making t: Pounding clay would still be tiring even with lighter loads.
why.A batch of pots would be completed in a: Several months were still needed to finish a batch.
why.She would receive more rupees for the sa: The payment of only a few rupees would not change merely because the loads were lighter.

activities.explanation: Lighter loads would place less strain on her back.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Arenla received very little money for the work involved in making a batch of pots.
Reason (R): The batch took several months to finish.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The months of work help explain why her payment of only a few rupees was so little.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Learning weaving could provide cloth for Arenla's family.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is true, but weaving could be done indoors in every season.

activities.prompt: How did making pots compare with learning weaving in terms of money, working conditions, and time?
activities.answer: Making pots required Arenla to travel to the riverbank, climb down a steep drop, and carry heavy loads uphill. The clay had to be pounded in bamboo cylinders, which was tiring, and the work took several months for one batch. She received only a few rupees for all this effort. Learning weaving was therefore more promising: it could earn more money and provide cloth for the family, could be done indoors in every season, and one shawl took less time than a batch of pots.
points: Pot-making involved heavy loads, tiring work, and several months.
Arenla received only a few rupees for a batch of pots.
Weaving could earn more money and provide cloth.
Weaving was possible indoors in every season and took less time for one shawl.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Arenla had a duty to teach Sentila.
Reason (R): Teaching Mesoba’s daughter was Arenla’s duty.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The second statement gives the reason the first statement is true.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The pots were dried in the sun before being taken to the kiln.
Reason (R): Over-firing and under-firing were safe ways to protect a batch from being ruined.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The first statement is true, but the second contradicts the danger to an entire batch.

activities.prompt: Explain why the council did not accept Mesoba’s claim that Arenla had never refused to teach Sentila as enough to settle the matter.
activities.answer: The council did not treat Arenla’s past willingness as a complete answer because Mesoba’s claim only showed that she had not refused. The council’s point was that teaching Sentila was Arenla’s duty as Mesoba’s daughter. It also held that traditional skills did not belong to one person and that experts were expected to pass their skills to anyone who wished to learn. Thus, Arenla’s response to Mesoba could not turn teaching into a personal favour or remove the village’s expectation that knowledge would be shared.
points: Mesoba’s claim showed only that Arenla had not refused.
Teaching Sentila was identified as Arenla’s duty.
Traditional skills were not to remain with one person.
Experts were expected to pass on their skills.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The following year, Arenla took Sentila to the riverbank and taught her to dig clay with a dao. She learned to put the right amount of clay into a bamboo cylinder and quickly turned it into malleable dough, but she could not hold the lump properly. She practised with Arenla for almost a year without learning. By custom, Sentila was sent to stay in a girls’ dormitory for some nights. Onula, the kind widow supervising the girls, resolved to help her.
activities.prompt: After Sentila reaches the girls’ dormitory, what should Onula do next, based on her decision to help Sentila?
options: She should look for further ways to help Sentila practise handling the clay.
She should stop all clay practice because Sentila did not learn for almost a year.
She should take over Arenla’s dao lesson at the riverbank.
She should have Sentila dig more clay with a dao instead of working on holding the dough.

why.She should stop all clay practice becaus: It contradicts Onula’s determination to help Sentila.
why.She should take over Arenla’s dao lesson: Arenla was the one who taught Sentila to dig clay with a dao.
why.She should have Sentila dig more clay wi: Digging clay was not Sentila’s main unresolved difficulty.

activities.explanation: This matches Onula’s decision to help in every possible way.

The dao was meant for holding dough rather than digging clay.
The bamboo cylinder was used only after Sentila had mastered handling dough.
The girls’ dormitory custom had interrupted her clay practice.

why.The dao was meant for holding dough rath: A dao was used for digging clay, not holding dough.
why.The bamboo cylinder was used only after: Sentila learned to use the bamboo cylinder before mastering the lump.
why.The girls’ dormitory custom had interrup: The passage does not identify this interruption as the cause of her continuing difficulty.

activities.explanation: Preparing the clay quickly and handling the lump were different difficulties.

why.The custom about Sentila’s nights at the: The dormitory custom existed independently of Onula’s feelings about Sentila.
why.Sentila would probably have learned to h: Sentila practised for almost a year without learning to hold the dough properly.

activities.explanation: Without Onula’s decision to help, Sentila would have had less support from the widow.

activities.prompt:

Reason (R): Her inability to hold the lump properly explains why she continued to need practice.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the handling difficulty explains the need for further practice.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Arenla taught Sentila to dig clay with a bamboo cylinder.
Reason (R): The riverbank visit gave Arenla a chance to teach Sentila to dig clay with a dao.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

activities.prompt: How did the difficulty in making the lump differ from the difficulty of preparing the clay?
activities.answer: Sentila made progress in the earlier stages of the work. She learned to place the correct amount of clay in a bamboo cylinder, and she could turn the clay into malleable dough quickly. The remaining difficulty was handling the finished lump, which she could not hold properly. Because this last step was still unsolved, she practised with Arenla for almost a year without learning it. The problem was therefore not in digging clay or preparing the right amount, but in controlling the lump of dough.

Connects the problem with almost a year of unsuccessful practice

lessons.title: Fans: names, history and trade

activities.prompt: What stories could a fan tell about the people who made and used it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a pankha?
activities.body: The word pankha names all kinds of fans. Pankh means a bird's feather. In ancient India, a pankhi was a small fan made with feathers. Ajanta wall paintings show pankhi use in India. They date to the 2nd century CE. Pankhas fanned holy figures in temples and kings at royal courts. They also became traded cultural goods. Today, they are mainly used for decoration.
keyPoints: Pankh means a bird's feather.
Pankhis were small fans used in ancient India.
Pankhas became traded goods and are now mainly decorative.
activities.explanation: You have learned the names, uses and trading history of pankhas.

activities.prompt: A child sees a large pankha at a temple and wonders why it was so hard to move.
steps: Some large pankhas needed a person’s full arm strength, so moving them was hard.
Temples used pankhas to fan deities, so the fan had a special purpose.
Royal courts used pankhas to fan kings, so the same object served another important role.
These uses explain why pankhas became important cultural goods.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The meaning of pankh
activities.prompt: What does the word ‘pankh’ mean?
options: A bird's feather
A village market
A royal court
A trade route
activities.explanation: Well done! Pankh means the feather of a bird.

activities.title: Name for all fans
activities.prompt: The word ______ is used for all kinds of fans.
activities.hint: This word names every kind of fan.
activities.explanation: Great choice! Pankha is the word used for all kinds of fans.

activities.title: Match the fan words
activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
activities.explanation: You matched all three words correctly. Their meanings are closely connected!

activities.title: Evidence at Ajanta
activities.prompt: What do the Ajanta wall paintings show?
options: Early pankhi use in India
Modern fan decoration
Large pankhas at courts
Pankhas on trade routes
activities.explanation: Correct! The paintings show evidence of pankhi use in India.

activities.title: Pankhas through time
activities.prompt: Put these stages of pankha history in order from earliest to latest.
items: Early pankhi use in India
Pankhas become traded goods
Modern use for decoration
activities.explanation: Nice ordering! Ajanta shows early use, trading came later, and decoration is the modern use.

activities.title: Trade and style
activities.prompt: Which pair of statements about pankhas is correct?
options: They were traded; people liked their style.
They were traded; only large pankhas were used.
They were local goods; people disliked their style.
They were decorations; people feared their style.
activities.explanation: Yes! Pankhas were traded along trade routes. People considered them exotic and stylish.

activities.prompt: A seller shows fans in several sizes and calls each one a pankha. What can the child infer?
options: Pankha is a general word for fans.
Pankha means only one tiny fan size.
Pankha means a bird’s soft covering.
Pankha means a wall painting at Ajanta.

This choice limits the word to one size, ignoring other fans.
This choice mixes the meaning of ‘pankh’ with ‘pankha’.
This choice mixes a fan word with a place where paintings appear.

activities.explanation: The seller uses ‘pankha’ for different fans, showing it is a general word.

activities.prompt: An old Indian picture shows a small fan with feathers, and Buddhist paintings at Ajanta include it. What can the child infer?
options: Pankhis were used in India in ancient times.
Pankhis were made only for temples.
Pankhis were mainly modern decorations.
Pankhis were too small to appear in art.

This choice mistakes one known use for the only possible use.
This choice mistakes modern decoration for the ancient use shown.
This choice assumes size stopped pankhis from appearing in paintings.

activities.explanation: The Ajanta paintings date to the 2nd century CE, showing ancient Indian use.

activities.prompt: Children see a fan in a temple and hear that a similar fan served in a royal court. What does this show?
options: Pankhas served important people and sacred spaces.
Pankhas were only used by ordinary families.
Pankhas were used mainly as trade goods.
Pankhas were used to paint temple walls.

why.Pankhas were only used by ordinary famil: This choice mistakes special uses for the only possible uses.
This choice focuses on trading and ignores the temple and court uses.
This choice confuses using fans near paintings with painting temple walls.

activities.explanation: Temples used pankhas to fan deities, and courts used them to fan kings.

activities.prompt: Traders carry pankhas along trade routes, and buyers praise them as exotic and stylish. What can the child conclude?
options: Pankhas were valued goods that travelled.
Pankhas were common items with no appeal.
Pankhas were mainly used for decoration then.
Pankhas were too large to move far.

why.Pankhas were common items with no appeal: This choice ignores the buyers’ interest in pankhas.
why.Pankhas were mainly used for decoration: This choice confuses modern decoration with their importance in trade.
This choice treats strength as proof that pankhas could not travel.

activities.explanation: Pankhas were traded along trade routes and considered exotic and stylish.

activities.prompt: In modern times, a family keeps a pankha at home but does not use it to cool the room. What most likely explains this?
options: Pankhas are mainly used as decoration now.
Pankhas are still needed to fan deities.
Pankhas are now made only for trade routes.
Pankhas are now used to fan kings daily.

This choice confuses a modern decorative use with an ancient temple use.
why.Pankhas are now made only for trade rout: This choice confuses trade routes with the main modern use.
This choice confuses a royal court use with modern family life.

activities.explanation: In modern times, pankhas are mainly used for decoration.

lessons.title: Regional pankhas

activities.prompt: What makes pankhas from different regions unique?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Hand fans around the regions
activities.body: Regional pankhas are hand fans with different designs and materials. In Rajasthan, appliqué joins shaped fabric pieces to another cloth with ornamental needlework. Zardozi uses glittering, encrusted gold thread, while temple fans use engraved brass and long handles. Gujarat has mirror-work cotton fans and colourful bead fans. Bengal uses sola and palm leaf, while Kutch makes hand-stitched leather fans.
keyPoints: Appliqué joins shaped fabric pieces with ornamental needlework.
Zardozi uses glittering and encrusted gold threadwork.
Gujarat has mirror-work cotton fans and colourful bead fans.
Bengal uses sola and palm leaf, while Kutch makes leather fans.
activities.explanation: Regional pankhas use different fabrics, materials and decorations.

activities.prompt: Which fan should a child choose to decorate a wall?
steps: The child wants a fan for wall decoration.
Gujarat’s dainty bead fans are commonly used as wall decorations.
So the child should choose Gujarat’s dainty bead fans.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which choice describes the pieces used in Rajasthan’s appliqué hand fan?
options: Fabric pieces with varied shapes
Brass pieces with smooth curves
Cardboard pieces with bright images
Leaf pieces with rough edges
activities.explanation: Appliqué hand fans use fabric pieces with different shapes and patterns.

activities.prompt: Rajasthan’s zardozi hand fan uses glittering and encrusted gold threadwork.
activities.explanation: Yes, glittering and encrusted gold threadwork makes the zardozi hand fan special.

activities.prompt: Rajasthan’s temple hand fans are made by engraving ______ and have long handles.
activities.hint: This metal is engraved to make the fans.
activities.explanation: Temple hand fans are made by engraving brass, and they have long handles.

activities.prompt: Which description fits Rajasthan’s temple hand fans?
options: Engraved brass with long handles
Painted wood with short handles
Woven cloth with round handles
Plain cardboard with no handles
activities.explanation: Rajasthan’s temple hand fans have engraved brass and long handles.

activities.prompt: Match each regional hand fan to its decoration or material.
pairs: Thread and wool at the seams
activities.explanation: Each fan has a distinctive material or decoration linked to its region.

activities.prompt: Which statement about regional hand fans is correct?
options: Gujarat’s dainty bead fans are wall decorations.
Bengal’s Tal Patar Pankhas are wall decorations.
Gujarat’s dainty bead fans are kept as household possessions.
Gujarat’s dainty bead fans are made with mirror work.
activities.explanation: Gujarat’s dainty bead fans are wall decorations. Tal Patar Pankhas are kept in Bengali households.

activities.prompt: Sita sees a fan with shaped fabric pieces sewn onto cloth. How does she most likely feel?
options: Impressed by the careful needlework
Worried that the cloth may tear
Angry that the pieces differ
Bored because the fan is plain

why.Worried that the cloth may tear: She may expect differently shaped pieces to be a sign of damage.
why.Angry that the pieces differ: She may think every fabric piece should look exactly the same.
why.Bored because the fan is plain: She may assume the patterned pieces are too quiet to notice.

activities.explanation: This fits because the varied shapes and ornamental stitching show careful decoration.

activities.prompt: Rhea repairs the edges of a Kutch fan. Which repair fits its design?
options: Stitch thread and wool along the seams
Fix bright mirrors onto a cotton base
Engrave brass with pictures and patterns
Glue colourful beads near a handle

why.Fix bright mirrors onto a cotton base: The child may mix Gujarat’s mirror work with Kutch’s leather work.
why.Engrave brass with pictures and patterns: The child may confuse brass engraving with stitched leather.
why.Glue colourful beads near a handle: The child may confuse bead decoration with seam stitching.

activities.explanation: This fits because Kutch fans are decorated with thread and wool at the seams.

activities.prompt: A Bengali family keeps a Tal Patar Pankha. What does this suggest?
options: It is a valued household possession.
It is likely used only outdoors.
It has no special place at home.
It is made from colourful beads.

The child may confuse a household possession with an outdoor object.
The child may think keeping it means the family does not value it.
The child may confuse palm leaf with bead decoration.

activities.explanation: This fits because Tal Patar Pankhas are kept in Bengali households as possessions.

activities.prompt: The description says the fan has glittering, encrusted gold threadwork. What does encrusted mean?
options: Covered with shiny decoration
Made from plain cardboard
Kept on a long handle
Made from soft leather

why.Made from plain cardboard: The child may confuse surface decoration with the material underneath.
why.Kept on a long handle: The child may confuse a handle feature with the word’s meaning.
why.Made from soft leather: The child may confuse Kutch’s leather with gold threadwork.

activities.explanation: This fits because encrusted gold threadwork means gold decoration covering the fan.

activities.prompt: A Phadh hand fan has gold, silver zari, silk and satin frills. What does this suggest?
options: It combines several decorative materials.
It uses one plain, simple material.
It is made from cardboard with images.
It is made from stitched leather

The child may overlook the several listed materials.
The child may confuse Phadh fans with Rajasthan’s painted cardboard fans.
why.It is made from stitched leather: The child may confuse Phadh fans with Kutch’s stitched leather fans.

activities.explanation: This fits because gold, zari, silk and satin show varied decoration.

lessons.title: Tribes and the changing craft

activities.prompt: How can we help a traditional fan craft survive and thrive?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the pankha craft is changing
activities.body: Tribal makers create handheld fans with metal, bamboo sticks and grass. Antique pieces use silk and brass. Their designs show geometrical patterns in white ink on red backgrounds. The pankha handicraft has now become a commercial business. This business gives some artisans a livelihood. Different crafted versions can increase demand. We can preserve this culture by celebrating pankhas, appreciating them and showing them at exhibitions.
keyPoints: Geometrical patterns use white ink on red backgrounds.
Commercial business supports some artisans.
Exhibitions can demonstrate the craft and regain popularity.
activities.explanation: The lesson explains how pankhas changed and how we can support their culture.

activities.prompt: A child sees fewer pankhas in daily life and asks how the craft can be protected.
steps: Celebrating pankhas is useful because it starts the work of preserving the craft.
Appreciating their culture matters because it helps keep this tradition present.
Makers can hold exhibitions because showing the craft may regain its popularity.
Therefore, families and makers can protect pankhas and support artisans' livelihoods.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which materials are used to make tribal handheld fans?
options: Metal, bamboo sticks and grass
Silk, bamboo sticks and grass
Metal, bamboo sticks and brass
Metal, silk and bamboo sticks
activities.explanation: Tribal makers use metal with bamboo sticks and grass.

activities.prompt: Tribal makers use geometrical patterns with red ink and white backgrounds.
activities.explanation: The patterns use white ink with red backgrounds.

activities.prompt: Antique pieces of tribal hand fans are kept with ______ and brass.
activities.hint: This material is used with brass for antique pieces.
activities.explanation: Silk and brass are kept for antique pieces of tribal hand fans.

activities.prompt: Match each material or feature with its use in pankhas.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how the materials and patterns are used.

activities.prompt: What does the pankha business now provide to some artisans?
options: Some form of livelihood
More demand for crafted pankhas
More antique pieces with silk and brass
More support for cultural celebrations
activities.explanation: The commercial business now gives some form of livelihood to India's artisans.

activities.prompt: The culture of pankhas may slowly lose its presence among Indians.
activities.explanation: The lesson says this culture may slowly lose its presence.

activities.prompt: A family wants the pankha craft to remain part of Indian life. What action best begins this work?
options: Celebrate pankhas and appreciate their culture.
Use bamboo and grass for every new fan.
Hide pankhas from public events and displays.
Sell every fan as an antique piece.

This confuses ordinary fan materials with cultural preservation.
why.Hide pankhas from public events and disp: This mistakes hiding the craft for protecting it.
This treats every fan as antique, even when it is not.

activities.explanation: This is right because celebration and appreciation begin preservation.

activities.prompt: An artisan is losing attention to pankhas. What can help bring the craft back into public view?
options: Hold an exhibition and show the craft.
Keep the craft hidden from the public.
Make every fan look exactly the same.
Stop showing how the fans are made.

This mistakes hiding the craft for gaining public interest.
This wrongly removes variety from the crafted pankhas.
This mistakes hiding the making process for showing the craft.

activities.explanation: This is right because exhibitions can demonstrate the craft and regain popularity.

activities.prompt: A hand fan is kept for an antique piece. What does the choice of silk and brass suggest?
options: It is treated as a special antique piece.
It is made for rough bamboo everyday work.
It uses only grass and simple sticks.
It is meant to lose its cultural value.

why.It is made for rough bamboo everyday wor: This confuses antique materials with bamboo-and-grass fan making.
This confuses simple fan materials with antique hand fans.
This reverses the idea that special pieces keep cultural value.

activities.explanation: This is right because silk and brass are kept for antique pieces.

activities.prompt: A maker offers several different crafted pankhas. Why might this help the business?
options: Different versions can increase demand for the craft.
Different versions make every fan antique.
Different versions reduce the need for paying artisans.
Different versions force buyers to choose one.

why.Different versions make every fan antiqu: This confuses variety in design with being antique.
why.Different versions reduce the need for p: This wrongly suggests more versions mean less need for artisans.
why.Different versions force buyers to choos: This assumes variety limits choices instead of helping demand.

activities.explanation: This is right because different versions help increase demand.

lessons.title: The Last Leaf

activities.prompt: Could one small act of kindness give someone the will to live?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Johnsy and the Last Leaf
activities.body: Johnsy became ill with pneumonia in November. She believed she would die when the last leaf fell. Sue called Behrman, a sixty-year-old painter, to model for her. During a storm, one leaf remained on the creeper. Behrman painted the last leaf on that stormy night. Johnsy realised that wanting to die was wrong. The doctor said she now wanted to live. Behrman died of pneumonia the next morning.
keyPoints: Johnsy believed she would die when the last leaf fell.
Behrman painted the last leaf on the stormy night.
The doctor saw that Johnsy now wanted to live.
activities.explanation: The last leaf brought hope to Johnsy, but Behrman paid a sad price.

activities.prompt: How can one painted leaf change a sick girl's mind?
steps: Johnsy linked the last leaf with death, so she watched it closely.
The creeper still showed a leaf because Behrman had painted one.
Johnsy saw that wanting death was wrong, so she chose life.
The doctor saw her will to live, while Behrman's death brought sorrow.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who did Sue call to model for her painting?
options: Johnsy
Behrman
Sue
The doctor
activities.explanation: Sue called Behrman to model for her painting.

activities.prompt: Behrman was a ______-year-old painter.
activities.hint: His age is given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Behrman was sixty years old.

activities.prompt: Match each person with what happened.
pairs: She believed she would die when the last leaf fell.
She called Behrman to model for a painting.
He painted the last leaf on the stormy night.
He said Johnsy now had the will to live.
activities.explanation: Each person played a different part in Johnsy’s story.

activities.prompt: Which things were found near Behrman’s bed?
options: A ladder and a lantern
A brush and a lantern
A ladder and a brush
A shoe and a lantern
activities.explanation: A ladder and a lighted lantern were found beside his bed.

activities.prompt: Why did Johnsy’s outlook change?
options: She realised that wanting to die was wrong.
She thought that all paintings were useless.
She wanted the doctor to leave her alone.
She decided to stay away from Behrman.
activities.explanation: Johnsy realised that wanting to die was wrong.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: Johnsy became ill in November.
Behrman painted the last leaf on the stormy night.
Behrman died of pneumonia the next morning.
activities.explanation: Johnsy became ill before the stormy night and Behrman’s death.

activities.prompt: One leaf stayed on the creeper during the storm. How did Johnsy feel?
options: She felt calm because the storm was over.
She feared that she might soon die.
She felt happy that one leaf stayed.
She wanted to paint the last leaf.

why.She felt calm because the storm was over: This fits Johnsy’s belief that the last leaf meant death.
She was afraid because the last leaf still remained.
She did not know that the leaf could be painted.

activities.explanation: She thought the last leaf falling meant she would die.

activities.prompt: Behrman’s clothes and shoes were wet, and he was shivering. What does this show?
options: He had been painting outside in the storm.
He had been hiding from the storm indoors.
He had been searching for a warm coat.
He had been waiting for Johnsy’s doctor.

why.He had been hiding from the storm indoor: Staying indoors would not explain his wet clothes and shivering.
A search for clothes does not explain the storm and wetness.
Waiting for a doctor does not explain the storm and wetness.

activities.explanation: His wet clothes and shivering suggest he was out in the storm.

activities.prompt: Sue called Behrman to be her model for a painting. What does “model” mean here?
options: The person being painted by an artist
The person who buys an artist's painting
The artist's painting of a leafy tree
The place where an artist keeps brushes

why.The person who buys an artist's painting: This confuses the model with the person buying the painting.
why.The artist's painting of a leafy tree: This confuses the model with the painting itself.
why.The place where an artist keeps brushes: This confuses the model with the artist's supplies.

activities.explanation: A model is the person whose image an artist paints.

activities.prompt: Behrman painted the last leaf on the stormy night. Why might he have done this?
options: To give Johnsy hope during her illness
To earn money from Sue's painting
To show that the storm had ended
To punish Johnsy for fearing death

why.To earn money from Sue's painting: Earning money is not suggested by the facts.
why.To show that the storm had ended: The stormy night did not show that the storm had ended.
why.To punish Johnsy for fearing death: Johnsy had not harmed Behrman, so punishment is unlikely.

activities.explanation: Johnsy found the will to live after seeing the painted leaf.

activities.prompt: Behrman died of pneumonia the next morning. Why is his death linked to the leaf?
options: He stayed outside in the storm to paint it
He caught his illness from Johnsy's doctor
He gave away his warm clothes to Johnsy
He forgot to return from Sue's house

why.He caught his illness from Johnsy's doct: The story does not say that he met Johnsy's doctor.
why.He gave away his warm clothes to Johnsy: The story does not say that he gave away his clothes.
why.He forgot to return from Sue's house: The story does not say that he went to Sue's house.

activities.explanation: The wet clothes, shivering, and painting show he faced the storm.

lessons.title: Canvas of Soil: poem and meaning

activities.prompt: How can a garden become a painting that tells us about life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Garden Becomes a Painting
activities.body: This poem turns a garden into a colourful painting. A painter mixes colours on a palette, and a hue means a shade of a colour. The earth becomes a rich, deep palette. Seeds are like brushstrokes, while each garden plot is like a wide canvas. Gardeners make still paintings. The garden shows art and life together. It can also act as an allegory, expressing ideas without stating them directly.
keyPoints: The earth is compared to a rich, deep palette.
Seeds, garden plots and blossoms become painting images.
The garden shows art and life together.
activities.explanation: This card helps you see how the poem joins gardening with painting.

activities.prompt: Why can a garden be like a painting?
steps: A painter mixes colours on a palette, so a picture can form.
The earth is a rich, deep palette, so it holds many colours.
Seeds act like brushstrokes, so spring helps the garden’s picture grow.
Each plot is a wide canvas, so gardens bring art and life together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Painter’s Tool
activities.prompt: A painter mixes colours on what?
options: garden plot
palette
canvas
brushstrokes
activities.explanation: Nice work! The painter mixes colours on a palette.

activities.title: Mixing Colours
activities.prompt: A painter mixes colours on a ______.
activities.hint: It is where the painter mixes colours.
activities.explanation: Exactly! A palette is where a painter mixes colours.

activities.title: Garden and Painting Pairs
activities.prompt: Match each garden or painting word to its partner.
activities.explanation: Great matching! The poem compares garden images with painting images.

activities.title: Seeds as Brushstrokes
activities.prompt: What does the poet compare the seeds to?
options: garden plots
hues
brushstrokes
palettes
activities.explanation: Yes! The poet compares seeds to brushstrokes in a painting.

activities.title: The Garden’s Deeper Meaning
activities.prompt: What can a garden with changing seasons represent?
options: life’s journey and growth
a hue and a shade
palette and canvas
blossoms and brushstrokes
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Changing seasons can represent life’s journey and growth.

activities.title: From Waiting to Blooming
activities.prompt: Put these stages of the garden’s spring in order.
items: Planted seeds wait
Spring’s vibrant colour
Blooming blossoms form a painted sight
activities.explanation: Well done! The poem moves from waiting seeds to spring’s colour and blossoms.

activities.prompt: Seeds are planted in a garden. They wait for spring’s vibrant colour. How might the gardener feel?
options: The gardener may feel excited about spring.
The gardener may feel worried about spring.
The gardener may feel bored by spring.
The gardener may feel angry at spring.

why.The gardener may feel worried about spri: This mistake reads waiting as worry.
This mistake reads waiting as boredom.
This mistake reads waiting as anger.

activities.explanation: The waiting for spring suggests anticipation and excitement.

activities.prompt: The poem compares seeds to brushstrokes. What does this suggest about the garden’s picture?
options: Seeds help create the garden’s changing picture.
Seeds remove every colour from the garden.
Seeds make the garden look completely empty.
Seeds stop the garden from changing at all.

why.Seeds remove every colour from the garde: This mistake thinks brushstrokes remove colour.
why.Seeds make the garden look completely em: This mistake thinks seeds make the garden empty.
why.Seeds stop the garden from changing at a: This mistake thinks brushstrokes stop all change.

activities.explanation: Seeds are like brushstrokes, so they help form the garden’s picture.

activities.prompt: Each garden plot is compared to a wide canvas. Why might gardeners turn gardens into still paintings?
options: To bring art and life together in the garden.
To keep every garden free of changing seasons.
To make seeds wait longer for spring’s colour.
To separate living gardens from painted art.

why.To keep every garden free of changing se: This mistake thinks gardens must avoid changing seasons.
why.To make seeds wait longer for spring’s c: This mistake thinks planting makes spring arrive later.
why.To separate living gardens from painted: This mistake thinks art and life must stay separate.

activities.explanation: Turning gardens into paintings joins art and life.

activities.prompt: A garden changes with the seasons. What larger idea might this change represent?
options: Life’s journey and growth over time.
A painter’s palette being left unused.
A song about colours losing their shades.
A gate that never opens for spring.

This mistake treats the garden as only an unused palette.
why.A song about colours losing their shades: This mistake treats the garden as a song about colours.
This mistake treats the garden as a gate for spring.

activities.explanation: Changing seasons can show life moving through growth.

activities.prompt: A garden shows many colours together. What idea can these colours represent?
options: The beauty of diversity and harmony.
The end of art in a garden.
The absence of life in a garden.
The danger of every changing season.

This mistake thinks the poem ends art in gardens.
This mistake thinks colourful gardens have no life.
This mistake thinks changing seasons must be dangerous.

activities.explanation: These colours can show diversity and harmony together.

lessons.title: Canvas of Soil: words and projects

activities.prompt: How could soil become a canvas for words and art?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Painters and garden projects
activities.body: Painters gathered around easels, which hold artwork. Each framed a canvas for painting. They played with shades and hues, colour differences. One student made a portrait, a picture of his friend showing his features. Underpainting means a first layer of colour. Another painted a Spring Day mural, a wall picture. It was placed on the classroom's right wall. The art room had energy. Garden projects offered research and design choices.
keyPoints: Painters framed canvases and used shades and hues.
One portrait was finished with underpainting and final colours.
Students choose garden research and design assignments.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects lively painting with garden research and design.

activities.prompt: How can I choose two garden assignments that fit the project?
steps: The rule allows any two assignments, so count your choices first.
Choose garden research because it can cover history, design, and cultural importance.
Choose a garden design because paper or digital tools can be used.
Research and design make two assignments, so the plan follows the rule.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Colours in the poem
activities.prompt: Which colours does the poet mention?
options: Shades of green, red and blue.
Shades of green only.
Shades of red only.
Shades of blue only.
activities.explanation: The poet mentions green, red and blue together.

activities.title: The Mural's Position
activities.prompt: The Spring Day mural was placed on the classroom's ______ wall.
activities.hint: The lesson gives one side of the classroom.
activities.explanation: The mural was placed on the classroom's right wall.

activities.title: Match the Art Details
activities.prompt: Match each art detail with its matching description.
pairs: Placed on the classroom's right wall
activities.explanation: Each match links a painting choice with the art described in the lesson.

activities.title: Garden Research Topics
activities.prompt: Which set contains the garden research topics?
options: Shades, hues and final colours.
History, design and cultural importance.
Canvas, easel and portrait.
Art room, mural and underpainting.
activities.explanation: Garden research can focus on history, design and cultural importance.

activities.title: Make the Portrait
activities.prompt: Put the portrait-making steps in order.
items: Frame a canvas
Apply careful underpainting
Add final colours
activities.explanation: The canvas was prepared first. Underpainting came before the final colours.

activities.title: Plan a Garden Project
activities.prompt: Which plan follows the garden project instructions?
options: Choose two assignments; research culture; design a garden.
Choose five assignments; research culture; design a garden.
Choose two assignments; research culture; study the classroom wall.
Choose two assignments; research easels; design a garden.
activities.explanation: The project asks for two assignments. Researching cultural importance and designing a garden are allowed choices.

activities.prompt: Young painters walk towards their easels as soon as art begins. How do they most likely feel?
options: I am excited to start painting.
I am nervous because the easels are broken.
I am bored because no canvas is ready.
I am angry because nobody will help me.

why.I am nervous because the easels are brok: This mistake treats eagerness as fear.
This mistake thinks eager movement means a lack of interest.
This mistake reads quick movement as anger.

activities.explanation: Their eager approach shows that they were excited to begin.

activities.prompt: Green, red, and blue are mentioned among the poet’s shades. What does this suggest about the paintings?
options: They may use many different kinds of colour.
They must use only these three colours.
They will all look exactly the same.
They cannot show any change in shade.

This mistake takes one list of colours as a complete limit.
This mistake assumes different shades will look identical.
This mistake thinks naming shades means they were never mixed.

activities.explanation: The mention of several shades suggests that many colours may appear.

activities.prompt: You notice careful underpainting before the final colours on a friend’s portrait. What does this suggest?
options: The student took care with the finished portrait.
The student skipped all work before the final colours.
The student painted only the friend’s bright clothes.
The student copied another painter’s final colours.

why.The student skipped all work before the: This mistake thinks underpainting is not part of the work.
why.The student painted only the friend’s br: This mistake assumes every detail shows clothes instead of features.
why.The student copied another painter’s fin: This mistake treats careful work as proof of copying.

activities.explanation: Careful underpainting and final colours show care in finishing the portrait.

activities.prompt: The art room is full of artistic energy while everyone paints. How might a visitor describe it?
options: The room feels lively and full of art.
The room feels quiet and completely empty.
The room feels dull because nobody is working.
The room feels still because all painting has stopped.

why.The room feels quiet and completely empt: This mistake reads artistic energy as silence.
why.The room feels dull because nobody is wo: This mistake thinks creative work means a lack of interest.
why.The room feels still because all paintin: This mistake assumes full artistic energy means painting has stopped.

activities.explanation: Artistic energy makes the busy art room feel lively and full of art.

activities.prompt: Research covers five famous Indian gardens. A new garden design is also chosen. Which plan follows the rule?
options: Both choices count as two assignments.
Only the garden research counts as an assignment.
Only the garden design counts as an assignment.
Neither choice counts toward the project.

why.Only the garden research counts as an as: This mistake counts research but forgets that a design can be an assignment.
why.Only the garden design counts as an assi: This mistake counts design but forgets that garden research can be an assignment.
why.Neither choice counts toward the project: This mistake thinks only artwork in the art room counts.

activities.explanation: Research and design are two assignments, so the plan follows the rule.
