lessons.title: Resilience, Advocacy and Determination

activities.prompt: How did Dr Malik turn obstacles into opportunities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Strength for Life
activities.body: Dr Malik was often underestimated. She needed physical strength and resilience to continue. Resilience means the mental strength to keep going. Her family and fortitude helped her move forward. Fortitude means inner strength. She treated challenges as chances to show her ability. Advocacy means speaking up for people you support. Sports can challenge stereotypes about disability. She supports women through outdoor sports. She believes youth is the voice of tomorrow.
keyPoints: Resilience is mental strength to keep going.
Advocacy is an important part of her mission.
She uses setbacks to show strength and move forward.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how she faced challenges and supported others.

activities.prompt: A child with a disability is told she cannot join an outdoor activity. How can she keep moving forward?
steps: She can lean on her family’s support because it gives her strength to move forward.
She can use her mental resilience because it helps her continue through difficulty.
She can treat the challenge as a chance to show what she can do.
By turning the obstacle into a stepping stone, she can move forward with determination.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What helped Dr Malik move forward?
options: Family support and her own fortitude
Less physical strength and less support
Underestimation and easier challenges
New sports goals and easy choices
activities.explanation: Good choice. Her family’s support and her own fortitude helped her move forward.

activities.prompt: The Paralympics gave Dr Malik a new lease of life.
activities.explanation: Exactly. They also helped her push her limits.

activities.prompt: How can sports support Dr Malik’s advocacy mission?
options: They can hide disability and protect stereotypes.
They can challenge stereotypes and change attitudes.
They can stop outdoor sports for everyone.
They can reduce support for disabled people.
activities.explanation: Good thinking. Sports can challenge stereotypes and change attitudes towards disability.

activities.prompt: What advice does Dr Malik give about a setback?
options: Keep it hidden from other people
Treat it as proof that you cannot win
Wait for an easier challenge to appear
Use it to show your strength
activities.explanation: Well done. She advises people to use every setback to show their strength.

activities.prompt: Dr Malik believes that youth is the voice of yesterday.
activities.explanation: Good check. She believes that youth is the voice of tomorrow.

activities.prompt: Put Dr Malik’s response to a challenge in order.
items: Treat the challenge as a chance
Show what she could do
Turn the obstacle into a stepping stone
Move forward
activities.explanation: Well done. She saw each challenge as a chance to show what she could do.

activities.prompt: A class underestimates a student before a sports activity. The student keeps trying. What does this show?
options: She does not have enough ability to lead.
She wants others to think highly of her.
She uses practice to show what she can do.
She expects the class to stop judging her.

why.She does not have enough ability to lead: This mistake assumes that being underestimated means she truly lacks ability.
This mistake focuses on pride instead of her determination.
why.She expects the class to stop judging he: This mistake wrongly reads her persistence as wanting others’ approval.

activities.explanation: This is right because she treats the challenge as a chance to show her ability.

activities.prompt: After a hard sports day, she felt tired but did not give up. What helped her continue?
options: physical strength
mental resilience
sports ability
easy confidence

why.physical strength: This mistake confuses body power with the strength to continue.
why.sports ability: This mistake focuses on sports skill instead of inner strength.
why.easy confidence: This mistake wrongly assumes she continued because the day was easy.

activities.explanation: This is right because mental resilience helped her continue through difficulty.

activities.prompt: A speaker says, ‘Each closed door can become a step forward.’ What does she mean?
options: Obstacles can help someone move ahead.
Closed doors should never be opened.
Moving ahead always causes another problem.
Steps are more useful than other support.

This mistake takes the image of a closed door too literally.
why.Moving ahead always causes another probl: This mistake wrongly assumes progress always creates more difficulty.
why.Steps are more useful than other support: This mistake wrongly separates progress from the support that makes it possible.

activities.explanation: This is right because she turned her obstacles into stepping stones.

activities.prompt: A disabled athlete joins a sports event. Some people first doubt her ability. What can sports change?
options: Sports can challenge unfair beliefs about disability.
Sports will make every athlete exactly alike.
Sports will remove the need for fair support.
Sports will make all unfair judgements vanish.

why.Sports will make every athlete exactly a: This mistake assumes sport makes people identical rather than changing attitudes.
why.Sports will remove the need for fair sup: This mistake wrongly suggests sport removes the need for support.
why.Sports will make all unfair judgements v: This mistake makes a possible attitude change sound like a total promise.

activities.explanation: This is right because sports can challenge stereotypes and change attitudes.

activities.prompt: Dr Malik supports women in outdoor sports. She also speaks for disabled people. Why does she do both?
options: She sees advocacy and empowerment as part of her mission.
She believes only skilled athletes should speak for others.
She wants outdoor sports to replace all other support.
She thinks disabled people need less help from others.

why.She believes only skilled athletes shoul: This mistake wrongly limits advocacy to skilled athletes.
why.She wants outdoor sports to replace all: This mistake assumes advocacy means replacing practical support.
why.She thinks disabled people need less hel: This mistake reverses her belief that disabled people can be as capable as others.

activities.explanation: This is right because advocacy and women’s empowerment are both parts of her mission.

lessons.sceneCaption: Adnan Safee with Deepa Malik, the first Indian woman to win a Paralympic medal.

lessons.title: Facts, Opinions and Cause and Effect

activities.prompt: Ready to uncover how facts, opinions, and cause and effect connect?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Facts, Opinions and Cause and Effect
activities.body: A fact is information that can be proved to be true. An opinion expresses a writer’s beliefs or perception. In the lesson, winning the Rio silver medal is a fact, while calling it a personal victory is an opinion. A change in how the world sees disabilities can inspire para-athletes. Paralympics show their talent and determination.
keyPoints: A fact can be proved true.
An opinion shows a writer’s beliefs or perception.
A change in perception can inspire para-athletes.
activities.explanation: A proved statement is a fact, while a personal belief is an opinion.

activities.prompt: A girl faces surgery. Adults expect a wheelchair. How should we understand that?
steps: The adults' expectation came after the surgery, because the operation shaped what they pictured.
An expectation is not a proved fact, because it shows what they thought would happen.
So the reader should treat it as their prediction, not as her certain future.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: An ______ expresses a writer’s beliefs or perception.
activities.hint: Think about a belief rather than proof.
activities.explanation: An opinion shows what a writer believes or perceives.

activities.prompt: Winning the Rio silver medal is presented as a fact.
activities.explanation: The lesson presents winning the Rio silver medal as a fact.

activities.prompt: Which statement is presented as an opinion?
options: Winning the Rio silver medal.
Paralympics display para-athletes’ talent.
Calling the medal a personal victory.
The surgery was followed by an expectation.
activities.explanation: Calling the medal a personal victory expresses a personal view.

activities.prompt: Why is the claim about her contribution presented as an opinion?
options: It states something proved true.
It says “It is believed”.
It names the Working Group.
It calls the medal a personal victory.
activities.explanation: The phrase “It is believed” presents a belief rather than proved information.

activities.prompt: Match each person or event with what the lesson says.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a person or event with its description in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What can a change in global perception of disabilities cause?
options: It can reduce para-athlete talent.
It can replace para-athlete determination.
It can inspire para-athletes.
It can change Working Group membership.
activities.explanation: The lesson says a change in perception can inspire para-athletes.

activities.prompt: A report calls Rio silver a personal victory. What does it show?
options: The writer sees it as personally important.
The medal result can be directly proved.
The athlete must expect a wheelchair.
The Working Group caused the victory.

This is true of the medal result, but not of the personal judgment.
An expectation about a wheelchair does not explain this medal phrase.
Nothing connects the Working Group to this victory.

activities.explanation: This expresses the writer's personal view, which is what an opinion does.

activities.prompt: A writer says, "It is believed" about someone's contribution. What does that mean?
options: The claim is offered, but not proved.
The claim is a directly checked fact.
The claim is the writer's personal memory.
The claim is certain because the wording sounds sure.

This wrongly assumes that the wording proves the claim.
why.The claim is the writer's personal memor: This confuses an opinion about a contribution with a memory.
why.The claim is certain because the wording: This mistakes confident wording for clear proof.

activities.explanation: The phrase signals belief, so the claim is framed as an opinion.

activities.prompt: A child watches para-athletes keep trying with great skill. Why might the child admire them?
options: Their talent and determination are clearly shown.
Their future wheelchair use is already certain.
Their Working Group contribution is directly proved.
Their belief about global change is a fact.

why.Their future wheelchair use is already c: This confuses an expectation with a certain outcome.
why.Their Working Group contribution is dire: This mixes separate facts with an unsupported claim.
why.Their belief about global change is a fa: This mistakes a belief for a proved fact.

activities.explanation: The Paralympics display the talent and determination of para-athletes.

activities.prompt: People begin to see disabilities differently around the world. What may happen to para-athletes?
options: They may feel inspired by the change.
They may lose their talent and determination.
They may stop showing their skills.
They may expect no change at all.

why.They may lose their talent and determina: This wrongly assumes that inspiration removes their qualities.
This reverses the possible effect of feeling inspired.
This denies the possible effect of a changed perception.

activities.explanation: A change in global perceptions can inspire para-athletes.

lessons.title: Words, Modal Verbs and Reported Speech

activities.prompt: How can tiny modal verbs change what we mean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Modal verbs and reported speech
activities.body: Modal auxiliaries can express ability, possibility, obligation and prediction. Use could for possibility or unreal ability. Unreal ability means an ability that is only imagined. Use should for probability or advice. Use would for a request or a past habit. Reported speech can use said, told or says. A comparison table places direct speech beside reported speech. Movement words include crawl, amble, walk, jog, sprint, run and creep.
keyPoints: Use could for possibility or unreal ability.
Use should for probability or advice.
Use would for a request or a past habit.
activities.explanation: This card gives you the main language patterns for the activities.

activities.prompt: A child cannot lift a bag now. A friend gives advice. The child then asks for help. Which modal words fit each part?
steps: Could fits the first part because the ability is not real now.
Should fits the second part because the friend gives advice.
Would fits the last part because the child makes a request.
These words fit each meaning, so the conversation is clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word appears in the list of movement words?
options: crawl
should
could
said
activities.explanation: Crawl appears in the lesson’s list of movement words. Good choice!

activities.prompt: You can use ______ to give advice.
activities.hint: This modal can also show probability.
activities.explanation: Should can express probability and give advice. Good choice!

activities.prompt: Match each modal verb with its meaning.
pairs: a request or a past habit
activities.explanation: Each modal matches the meaning listed in the lesson. You matched them well!

activities.prompt: Which group lists all the reporting verbs?
options: said, told, says
crawl, walk, jog
could, should, would
crawl, amble, jog
activities.explanation: Said, told and says are the listed reporting verbs. Excellent grouping!

activities.prompt: Which opening is given for the interviewer’s reported sentence?
options: The interviewer said that
The interviewer said sports
The interviewer told that
The sports said that
activities.explanation: The reported sentence begins with “The interviewer said that”. Good choice!

activities.prompt: Which change is shown in Dr Malik’s reported speech?
options: “I love sports” becomes “she loved sports”
“I love sports” stays “I love sports”
“she loved sports” becomes “I love sports”
“I loved sports” becomes “she love sports”
activities.explanation: The lesson changes “I love sports” into “she loved sports”. Good choice!

activities.prompt: A child says, “I could lift it then, but not now.” What does could mean here?
options: An ability that is not true now.
A duty that the child must do.
A likely event in the near future.
A request for somebody else to act.

The sentence shows an ability, not a duty.
The sentence shows an ability, not a prediction.
The sentence shows an ability, not a request.

activities.explanation: This matches could for an ability that is not real now.

activities.prompt: A friend has a test tomorrow. You say, “You should study tonight.” What does should do here?
options: It gives advice about what to do.
It shows that something is likely.
It shows an ability that is not real.
It describes a past action done daily.

The sentence gives advice, not probability.
The sentence gives advice, not unreal ability.
The sentence gives advice, not a past habit.

activities.explanation: This fits should because it gives advice.

activities.prompt: A child says, “Would you please close the door?” What does would do here?
options: It makes a polite request of someone.
It gives advice about a possible choice.
It describes an action repeated in the past.
It predicts something that may happen later.

The speaker is asking, not giving advice.
why.It describes an action repeated in the p: There is no past habit in this sentence.
why.It predicts something that may happen la: The speaker is asking, not predicting.

activities.explanation: Would is used here to make a request.

activities.prompt: A child drops a cup and says, “It couldn’t be helped.” What is the child saying?
options: The problem could not be helped.
The problem was easy to help.
The child must help it at once.
The child wants to help it later.

Couldn’t means the opposite of being able to help it.
The sentence does not give the child a duty.
The sentence does not mention a later action.

activities.explanation: It uses couldn’t for something that could not be helped.

activities.prompt: A table places “I love sports” beside “She loved sports.” What change can the reader see?
options: The direct love becomes the reported loved.
The direct love stays exactly love.
The direct sports becomes the reported she.
The direct she becomes the reported I.

The reported sentence uses loved, not love.
why.The direct sports becomes the reported s: The reported sentence keeps sports and changes the speaker.
The direct sentence uses I, while the report uses she.

activities.explanation: The direct love changes to loved in the reported sentence.

lessons.title: Notices and the History of the Paralympics

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered why school notices matter and how the Paralympics began?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Notices and Paralympic History
activities.body: A notice passes information to students or another group. It may announce an event, celebration, competition or important news. A notice includes the organisation, date, heading, details and signature. The origin of the Paralympics can be traced back to 1948. Sir Ludwig Guttmann organised a sports competition for war veterans with spinal cord-related injuries.
keyPoints: Notices pass information to students or a particular group.
A notice includes an organisation, date, heading, details and signature.
The Paralympics' origin can be traced back to 1948.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas in notices and the early Paralympic history.

activities.title: Nine Runners, One Team
activities.body: Nine determined athletes waited at the starting line. The smallest runner stumbled and fell. The eight others turned back and helped him to his feet. Then all nine joined hands and continued together. They received gold medals. The spectators gave them a standing ovation, which means applause while standing. Special Olympics provides sports training and athletic competition.
keyPoints: The eight other runners stopped and helped the fallen boy.
All nine runners joined hands and continued together.
Special Olympics provides sports training and athletic competition.
activities.explanation: The runners showed unity by helping one another and continuing together.

activities.prompt: Why do eight runners stop when the smallest runner falls?

The race ends with nine gold medals, showing the value of unity.

activities.title: Unity and Special Olympics
activities.body: Special Olympics provides sports training and athletic competition. Its participants include children and adults with intellectual disabilities. It works to create a better world through acceptance and inclusion. The nine athletes joined hands and continued together. Their story shows unity between the runners. A collocation is a pair or group of words that habitually appear together.
keyPoints: Special Olympics provides sports training and athletic competition.
It works to create a better world through acceptance and inclusion.
A collocation is a pair or group of words that habitually appear together.

turned back and helped him up

why.They value speed, even when one runner f: This mistake ignores their choice to stop and help.
why.They value leaving the fallen runner beh: This mistake believes they continued without caring for him.

activities.context: At 29, Dr Deepa Malik was diagnosed with a spine tumour. Her illness left her paralysed from her waist downwards, and the doctors told her that she would use a wheelchair for life. She chose para-athletics after enjoying swimming. In 2016, she won shot-put silver at the Rio Paralympic Games and became India’s first female Paralympic medallist. Her awards include the Khel Ratna, Arjuna and Padma Shri.
activities.prompt: What does the contrast between the doctors’ prediction and Dr Malik’s later achievement show?
options: The prediction did not prevent her from competing and winning a Paralympic medal.
The prediction guaranteed that she would win a Paralympic medal.
Her medical condition made competition impossible after the diagnosis.
She recovered fully before she began para-athletics.

why.The prediction guaranteed that she would: The doctors predicted wheelchair use, not a Paralympic medal.
why.Her medical condition made competition i: She competed and won despite being paralysed from her waist downwards.
why.She recovered fully before she began par: No complete recovery is mentioned; her illness had left her paralysed.

activities.explanation: Her later medal shows that the prediction did not end her sporting journey.

activities.context: At 29, Dr Deepa Malik was diagnosed with a spine tumour. Her illness left her paralysed from her waist downwards, and the doctors told her that she would use a wheelchair for life. She chose para-athletics after enjoying swimming. In 2016, she won shot-put silver at the Rio Paralympic Games and became India’s first female Paralympic medallist. Her awards include the Khel Ratna, Arjuna and Padma Shri.
activities.prompt: If another athlete faced a physical limitation, which response would best follow Dr Malik’s example?
options: Treat the limitation as important while continuing to discover what the person can achieve.
Treat the limitation as proof that competitive sport is no longer possible.
Avoid all sport so that the limitation cannot affect performance.
Wait for a doctor’s prediction to settle the person’s future potential.

why.Treat the limitation as proof that compe: Dr Malik competed and won despite her paralysis.
why.Avoid all sport so that the limitation c: Avoiding sport would not follow her example of pursuing para-athletics.
why.Wait for a doctor’s prediction to settle: Her achievement shows that a doctor’s prediction need not determine her future.

activities.explanation: Her example shows that a physical limitation need not decide a person’s potential.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The doctors told Dr Deepa Malik that she would use a wheelchair for life.
Reason (R): Her illness left her paralysed from her waist downwards, explaining the doctors’ prediction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Her paralysis from the waist downwards explains why the doctors predicted lifelong wheelchair use.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Dr Deepa Malik chose para-athletics after enjoying swimming.
Reason (R): She chose para-athletics because the doctors prevented her from swimming.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is true, but the reason is false because her choice followed her enjoyment of swimming.

activities.prompt: Explain how Dr Deepa Malik’s medical situation and interest in swimming influenced her later achievement.
activities.answer: At 29, Dr Deepa Malik was diagnosed with a spine tumour. Her illness left her paralysed from her waist downwards, and the doctors told her that she would use a wheelchair for life. However, she did not let that prediction determine her potential. She chose para-athletics after enjoying swimming and went on to win shot-put silver at the 2016 Rio Paralympic Games. She became India’s first female Paralympic medallist. Her belief that physical limitations do not decide a person’s potential explains why she continued and succeeded.
points: She was diagnosed at 29 with a spine tumour.
Her illness left her paralysed from the waist downwards.
She chose para-athletics after enjoying swimming.
She won 2016 Rio shot-put silver and became India’s first female Paralympic medallist.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Dr Malik was often underestimated by others. To continue, she needed physical strength and mental resilience, while her family’s support and her own fortitude helped her move forward. She treated each challenge as a chance to show what she could do and turned her obstacles into stepping stones. The Paralympics gave her a new lease of life and helped her push her limits. She considers advocacy an important part of her mission.
activities.prompt: If Dr Malik could no longer receive her family’s support, which approach would best help her move forward?
options: Draw on inner strength and keep taking the next step
Rely on physical power alone and ignore mental toughness
Wait for other people to remove every obstacle
Accept the underestimated view and stop trying

why.Rely on physical power alone and ignore: She needed mental resilience as well as physical strength.
why.Wait for other people to remove every ob: She used obstacles as stepping stones rather than waiting.
why.Accept the underestimated view and stop: She kept going despite being underestimated.

activities.explanation: Her own fortitude helped her move forward.

activities.context: Dr Malik was often underestimated by others. To continue, she needed physical strength and mental resilience, while her family’s support and her own fortitude helped her move forward. She treated each challenge as a chance to show what she could do and turned her obstacles into stepping stones. The Paralympics gave her a new lease of life and helped her push her limits. activities.prompt: If a school used outdoor sports to bring disabled and able-bodied participants together, what result would best fit the lesson?
options: It could leave stereotypes unchanged and keep the groups separate
It could prove that only able-bodied people belong in sport

It could make disability a reason for avoiding outdoor activity

why.It could leave stereotypes unchanged and: Sports can change attitudes rather than leave them unchanged.
why.It could prove that only able-bodied peo: This contradicts Dr Malik’s belief in disabled people’s capability.
why.It could make disability a reason for av: This would work against the positive role described for sport.

activities.explanation: Sports can challenge stereotypes and change attitudes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Dr Malik sees advocacy as a way to support the recognition of disabled people as capable.
Reason (R): She believes disabled people can be as capable as able-bodied people and considers advocacy important to her mission.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true because her belief in disabled people’s capability helps explain why she values advocacy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Dr Malik believed that physical strength alone was enough for her to continue.
Reason (R): She needed both physical strength and mental resilience to continue.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because she needed mental resilience too, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between resilience and advocacy in Dr Malik’s mission.
activities.answer: Resilience is the strength to continue when difficulties arise. Dr Malik needed both physical strength and mental resilience to continue. Her family’s support and her own fortitude helped her move forward, and she turned obstacles into stepping stones. Advocacy is part of her effort to support disabled people and encourage empowerment, especially for women through outdoor sports and adventure activities. She believes disabled people can be as capable as able-bodied people. Therefore, resilience helps her overcome challenges, while advocacy helps her support disabled people and encourage women’s empowerment through outdoor activities.
points: Resilience means continuing despite difficulties.
Dr Malik needed both physical strength and mental resilience.
Her family’s support and own fortitude helped her move forward.
Advocacy supports disabled people and women through outdoor activities.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After Dr Deepa Malik's surgery, it was expected that she would use a wheelchair. She was a member of the Working Group. They could be inspired to expect that all athletes will use wheelchairs.

why.They could be inspired to reject the Wor: Nothing in the case connects the change to rejecting the Working Group.
why.They could be inspired to expect that al: The case does not say that all athletes will use wheelchairs.

activities.context: After Dr Deepa Malik's surgery, it was expected that she would use a wheelchair. She was a member of the Working Group. Her Rio silver medal is presented as a fact, while calling it a personal victory is presented as an opinion. Her contribution is described with the phrase “It is believed”. At the Paralympics, para-athletes display talent and determination, and a change in the global perception of disabilities can inspire them.
activities.prompt: What should a student do with the statement that calling the Rio silver medal a personal victory is an opinion?
options: Label it as an opinion because it expresses a belief or perception.
Label it as a fact because a medal can be proved.
Label it as an opinion only if it mentions the Working Group.
Label it as a fact because it refers to a medal.

why.Label it as a fact because a medal can b: The statement about a personal victory is presented as an opinion.
why.Label it as an opinion only if it mentio: The Working Group is not the reason for the classification.
why.Label it as a fact because it refers to: Referring to a medal does not make this wording a fact.

activities.explanation: This correctly applies the definition of an opinion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Winning the Rio silver medal is presented as a fact.
Reason (R): A fact is information that can be proved to be true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why the medal result is presented as a fact.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Calling the medal a personal victory is presented as an opinion.
Reason (R): The statement can be proved to be true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason wrongly treats an opinion as a provable fact.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a fact and an opinion using the case.
activities.answer: A fact is information that can be proved to be true. In the case, the Rio silver medal is presented as a fact because it gives a result that can be treated as provable. Calling the medal a personal victory is an opinion because it expresses a belief or perception, not simply a statement that can be checked. The claim about Dr Deepa Malik's contribution is also an opinion because it uses the phrase “It is believed”. That wording signals what people think. Therefore, the distinction depends on whether the statement gives provable information or presents a belief or perception.
points: Defines a fact as information that can be proved true.
Explains that the Rio silver medal is presented as a fact.
Explains that calling it a personal victory is an opinion.
Uses “It is believed” to explain another opinion.

activities.explanation: The lesson says that Shruti looks distressed at the end of the rehearsal.

activities.title: A Newspaper Clue
activities.prompt: The newspaper says that music runs in Shruti's ______.
activities.hint: This word comes from the newspaper's description.
activities.explanation: The newspaper says that music runs in Shruti's veins.

activities.title: Choose the True Pair
activities.prompt: Which pair of details about Shruti is true?
options: She looks distressed, and her father knows about the concert.
She looks distressed, and her father does not know about the concert.
She looks excited, and her father does not know about the concert.
She looks excited, and her father knows about the concert.
activities.explanation: Shruti looks distressed, and she has not told her father about the concert.

activities.prompt: Four children play together, and their Indo-Western fusion piece grows louder. How may the growing volume affect the performance?
options: It may make the performance feel more exciting and strong.
It may make the performance feel slower and more peaceful.
It may show that only one child is still playing.
It may mean that the children have stopped following the music.

why.It may make the performance feel slower: This mistakes louder music for a slower and calmer mood.
why.It may show that only one child is still: This mistakes a louder group performance for fewer performers.
why.It may mean that the children have stopp: This assumes louder playing means the children stopped following the music.

activities.explanation: The growing loudness suggests more energy and power in the performance.

activities.prompt: Shruti packs her violin after the rehearsal and looks distressed. How does she probably feel?
options: She feels worried about something connected with the concert.
She feels joyful because the noisy performance has ended.
She feels angry because the other children played together.
She feels bored because the concert has not started yet.

why.She feels joyful because the noisy perfo: This mistakes the end of a rehearsal for a happy celebration.
why.She feels angry because the other childr: This assumes playing together would make Shruti angry.
why.She feels bored because the concert has: This treats distress as boredom without evidence from the facts.

activities.explanation: Her worried face and the untold concert point to this feeling.

activities.prompt: During the rehearsal, Indian and Western music styles meet in one piece. What does "fusion" mean here?
options: It means bringing two different musical styles together.
It means keeping two different musical styles apart.
It means choosing one musical style and ignoring another.
It means changing styles without any clear musical plan.

why.It means keeping two different musical s: This mistakes fusion for keeping musical styles apart.
why.It means choosing one musical style and: This mistakes fusion for choosing one style and rejecting another.
why.It means changing styles without any cle: This mistakes fusion for music with no clear musical plan.

activities.explanation: Fusion means joining two different musical styles in one piece.

activities.prompt: A newspaper says that music runs in Shruti’s veins. What does this line imply?
options: Music is a deep and natural part of Shruti.
Music is something that Shruti does not really enjoy.
Music is something that Shruti learned very recently.
Music is a game Shruti plays with her friends.

why.Music is something that Shruti does not: This takes the metaphor to mean she does not enjoy music.
why.Music is something that Shruti learned v: This mistakes a natural gift for something learned recently.
why.Music is a game Shruti plays with her fr: This mistakes a description of her nature for a social game.

activities.explanation: The metaphor suggests music is naturally deep inside Shruti.

activities.prompt: After the rehearsal, the boys describe Shruti as a sensation. What do they mean?
options: They think her musical talent is wonderful and unusual.
They think she is worried about performing for her father.
They think her musical talent is simple and easy to copy.
They think she has told her father about the concert.

why.They think she is worried about performi: This mistakes praise for a statement about Shruti’s feelings.
why.They think her musical talent is simple: This mistakes admiration for a claim that her talent is ordinary.
why.They think she has told her father about: This confuses the boys’ praise with news about her father.

activities.explanation: The praise shows that her musical talent strongly impresses the boys.

activities.prompt: Shruti has not told her father about the concert, and she looks distressed. What may be troubling her?
options: She may be worried about telling her father about the concert.
She may be worried that the newspaper has stopped praising her.
She may be worried that the boys will forget her name.
She may be worried that nobody will bring instruments to the concert.

why.She may be worried that the newspaper ha: This mistakes newspaper praise for the likely cause of distress.
why.She may be worried that the boys will fo: This mistakes the boys’ praise for a problem about her name.
why.She may be worried that nobody will brin: This invents a problem about instruments that the facts do not show.

activities.explanation: The concert she has not mentioned is the clearest clue to her worry.

lessons.title: Act II: Shruti Tells Her Parents

activities.prompt: How will Shruti find the courage to speak with her father?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Serious Family Talk
activities.body: After dinner, Shruti’s parents clean the table while she sits with the last bite. Nabin tells her she must eat the dosa. Shruti finds the right words for her father. He agrees to listen, but cannot promise to stay calm. He allows one performance every six months, because too many can lead to contempt. He worries an orchestra may hide a performer’s individual style. Shruti promises her mother not to hide again.
keyPoints: Nabin tells Shruti to eat the dosa.
Nabin agrees to listen, but may not remain calm.
Shruti promises not to hide anything again.
activities.explanation: This scene shows Shruti’s honesty, Nabin’s concern, and their family talk.

activities.prompt: How should Shruti speak to Nabin about the group concert?
steps: She should plan her words, because she is trying to find them.
She should mention the group plan, because orchestras can hide individual style.
She should mention the limit, because many performances can lead to contempt.
She should speak carefully and listen, because Nabin may not promise calmness.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does Nabin tell Shruti?
options: She must eat the dosa.
She should leave the table.
She should stop speaking.
She should sing alone.
activities.explanation: Nabin tells Shruti that she must eat the dosa. He says that only staring at it is not enough.

activities.prompt: Nabin says that only staring at the ______ is not enough.
activities.hint: Think about the food Shruti is looking at.
activities.explanation: Nabin says that only staring at the dosa is not enough. He tells Shruti to eat it.

activities.prompt: Shruti has already finished every bite of her dinner.
activities.explanation: Shruti is still sitting with the last bite of her food. Her parents have started cleaning the table.

activities.prompt: What does Nabin agree to do?
options: Listen to Shruti.
Remain calm at all times.
Allow many more performances.
Perform in the orchestra.
activities.explanation: Nabin agrees to listen to Shruti. He will not promise to remain calm.

activities.prompt: Put these lesson moments in page order.
items: Nabin says only staring is not enough.
Nabin agrees to listen but will not promise calm.
Shruti promises not to hide anything again.
activities.explanation: These moments appear on pages 175, 176, and 177, in that order.

activities.prompt: Which concern fits the group concert and Nabin’s views on fusion music?
options: An orchestra may hide her individual style.
Her speech may hide her individual style.
The dosa may hide her individual style.
Her promise may hide her individual style.
activities.explanation: The upcoming concert is a group performance. Nabin believes an orchestra can hide a performer’s individual style.

activities.prompt: Shruti searches for the right words to speak. Nabin agrees to listen but may not stay calm. How does she feel?
options: She feels nervous about speaking to him.
She feels angry about the table cleanup.
She feels excited about eating her dosa.
She feels calm about his possible reaction.

She is not shown to be angry about the cleanup.
Nothing suggests that she feels excited about the dosa.
why.She feels calm about his possible reacti: His uncertain reaction means calmness would be unlikely.

activities.explanation: Her search for words shows hesitation and nervousness.

activities.prompt: Her parents clean the table after dinner. Shruti still sits with her last bite. Nabin says staring at the dosa is not enough. Why must she eat it?
options: He wants her to finish her dinner.
He wants her to begin a performance.
He wants her to clean the table.
He wants her to speak to her mother.

He is discussing dinner, not asking for a performance.
Cleaning the table is her parents' task, not his request.
His words concern Shruti's food, not communication with her mother.

activities.explanation: She still has food left, and he wants her to eat it.

activities.prompt: Nabin allows one performance every six months. He believes too many performances can lead to contempt. What may result?
options: They may begin to lose respect.
They may begin to feel afraid.
They may begin to feel surprised.
They may begin to feel more loved.

Fear is not the result explained by Nabin.
Surprise is not the result explained by Nabin.
More love does not match the meaning of contempt.

activities.explanation: Contempt here means losing respect for the performers.

activities.prompt: The upcoming concert is a group performance. Nabin says an orchestra can drown a performer's individual style. What worries him?
options: The performer's own style may disappear.
The performer's own style may grow stronger.
The orchestra may stop playing together.
The concert may become less crowded.

why.The performer's own style may grow stron: The fact says the style may be hidden, not strengthened.
His worry concerns the performer, not the orchestra working together.
No fact says that the concert will have fewer people.

activities.explanation: A strong orchestra can hide the performer's individual style.

activities.prompt: Nabin has stated his views on fusion music several times. What may be his purpose?
options: So Shruti understands his concern clearly.
So Shruti forgets the concert plan.
So her parents stop cleaning the table.
So she promises another performance.

Nothing suggests that he wants her to forget the concert.
The table cleanup is unrelated to his music views.
His performance limit does not promise her another show.

activities.explanation: Repeating his views may help Shruti understand his concern.

activities.prompt: Shruti promises her mother that she will not hide anything again. What does this show?
options: She wants to be honest with her parents.
She wants to keep every secret forever.
She wants to avoid speaking at meals.
She wants to perform more often.

A promise to be open does not mean keeping every secret.
She is agreeing to speak, not avoiding conversation.
Nothing links her promise to performing more often.

activities.explanation: Her promise shows that she wants honesty with her parents.

lessons.title: Act III: Music Changes Nabin’s Mind

activities.prompt: What changes Nabin’s mind about Shruti and the children’s music?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nabin Changes His Mind
activities.body: The final practice takes place at Iqbal’s house. Shruti hopes to practise the piece one last time. She considers telling the group that she cannot join the performance. Her parents enter the room and stand in a corner. Nabin claps furiously, looks proud, and praises the children. He praises Shruti’s perfect notes and plans a music room.
keyPoints: Shruti considers leaving the performance.
Nabin praises Shruti’s perfect notes.
Nabin plans a music room.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the final practice and Nabin’s change of heart.

activities.prompt: Why does Nabin come to understand Shruti’s choice after the final practice?
steps: Shruti practises with care, because she hopes to perform once more.
Her doubt has a reason, because she has thought about leaving.
Both help him, because music shows skill and Leela explains her doubt.
So he understands her choice, because music and explanation make sense together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where does the final practice take place?
options: At Iqbal’s house
At Leela’s house
At Nabin’s house
At Shruti’s house
activities.explanation: The final practice takes place at Iqbal’s house, so that is correct.

activities.prompt: Nabin comes from a family of ______.
activities.hint: This word names people who sing.
activities.explanation: Nabin comes from a family of vocalists, so the missing word is vocalists.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the lesson with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an event or person with the detail given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Whose help helps Nabin understand Shruti’s choice?
options: Leela’s help
Iqbal’s help
The parents’ help
The children’s help
activities.explanation: Nabin admits that Leela helped him understand Shruti’s choice.

activities.prompt: Which choice shows that Nabin now supports the children’s music?
options: He praises Shruti and plans a room
He blames Shruti and stops their music
He ignores Shruti and leaves the room
He cancels music and leaves the room
activities.explanation: Nabin praises Shruti and plans a music room, showing support for the children’s music.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen during the final practice.
items: Shruti hopes to practise once more.
Shruti considers leaving the performance.
Her parents enter and stand nearby.
Nabin claps and looks proud.
Nabin praises the children and Shruti.
activities.explanation: The order moves from Shruti’s thoughts to her parents’ arrival, applause, and praise.

activities.prompt: At Iqbal’s house, Shruti hopes to practise once more. She thinks about saying she cannot join. How does she most likely feel?
options: She feels torn about taking part in the performance.
She feels certain that she should leave the group.
She feels happy because the final practice is over.
She feels calm because nobody will notice her playing.

why.She feels certain that she should leave: This mistakes hesitation for certainty, but she is not certain.
why.She feels happy because the final practi: This assumes she is happy, but her thoughts show doubt.
why.She feels calm because nobody will notic: This assumes she ignores others, but she joins the practice.

activities.explanation: Her wish to practise and thought of leaving show mixed feelings.

activities.prompt: Nabin calls the children’s performance ‘soulful’ and praises Shruti’s perfect raga notes. What does ‘soulful’ mean here?
options: The music expresses strong, deep feeling.
The music is played much more quickly.
The music uses many different instruments.
The music is louder than every other sound.

This confuses feeling with speed, but praise does not concern speed.
why.The music uses many different instrument: This confuses feeling with instruments, but the word does not name them.
why.The music is louder than every other sou: This confuses feeling with loudness, but the word does not mean loud.

activities.explanation: ‘Soulful’ means full of deep feeling, which fits Nabin’s praise.

activities.prompt: Shruti is unsure about joining. Her parents enter the room and stand in a corner. What do their actions suggest?
options: They are leaving the practice at once.
They are quietly watching the situation unfold.
They are asking the children to stop.
They are bringing equipment for practice.

This mistakes standing for leaving, but the parents remain in the room.
This assumes they speak, but no request to stop is given.
why.They are bringing equipment for practice: This mistakes their arrival for bringing new equipment.

activities.explanation: Standing in a corner suggests they stay and quietly watch.

activities.prompt: Nabin says Leela helped him understand Shruti’s choice. What does this show about Leela’s role?
options: She arranged the final practice at Iqbal’s house.
She gave the children their new music equipment.
She explained something important about Shruti’s choice.
She made Nabin forget Shruti’s musical skill.

why.She arranged the final practice at Iqbal: This mistakes help for arranging, but no such task is given.
why.She gave the children their new music eq: This mistakes explanation for giving, but no equipment is mentioned.
why.She made Nabin forget Shruti’s musical s: This mistakes understanding for forgetting, which means the opposite.

activities.explanation: Leela’s help gave Nabin a clearer understanding of Shruti.

activities.prompt: Nabin comes from a family of vocalists. He plans a music room with more equipment for regular practice. What do these facts suggest?
options: His family believes music practice is no longer useful.
His family wants children to stop learning raga notes.
His family thinks a music room is unnecessary.
His family understands the value of steady music practice.

why.His family believes music practice is no: This reverses the meaning, because the plan supports more practice.
why.His family wants children to stop learni: This mistakes learning for stopping, but the plan helps practice.
why.His family thinks a music room is unnece: This treats the room as useless, but more equipment supports practice.

activities.explanation: Vocalists sing, and his plan values steady musical practice.

activities.prompt: Nabin praises the soulful performance and Shruti’s perfect raga notes. Leela helps him understand her choice. What does this show about his change of mind?
options: He now thinks Shruti should never sing again.
He now understands Shruti’s choice more clearly.
He now wants the children to leave the group.
He now believes Leela chose the wrong raga.

why.He now thinks Shruti should never sing a: This turns understanding into rejection, but nothing suggests rejection.
why.He now wants the children to leave the g: This invents a wish to end the group, but none is given.
why.He now believes Leela chose the wrong ra: This invents a different raga, while Leela actually helps him.

activities.explanation: The praise and Leela’s help both deepen his understanding.

lessons.title: Understanding the Play and Its Language

activities.prompt: How does music help a family listen, understand, and grow closer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Play’s Story and Language
activities.body: After Shruti performs, Nabin claps furiously and shows pride. He praises her instead of criticising her. Leela helps him understand Shruti’s musical choice. He admits he had underestimated his own music. Shruti wants to give fusion music a fair try. She does not know how to speak to her father properly. The play uses asides, non-lexical fillers, notes and crescendo.
keyPoints: Nabin responds with pride and praise.
Shruti wants a fair try with fusion music.
The play uses asides, fillers, notes and crescendo.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect the play’s action with its special speech forms.

activities.prompt: Shruti wants to try fusion music. She feels unsure about talking to her father. Why might she practise once and plan to leave?
steps: A fair trial matters because she wants to test the music.
She plans to practise once because she is not fully committed.
Talking is difficult because she does not know the right way.
So she may approach the music carefully without making a firm promise.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does Nabin do after hearing Shruti perform?
options: He leaves the group.
He claps furiously.
He criticises her performance.
He stays completely silent.
activities.explanation: Nabin claps furiously and wears an expression of pride.

activities.prompt: Leela helps Nabin understand his daughter’s ______ choice.
activities.hint: It describes the kind of music Shruti has chosen.
activities.explanation: Leela helps Nabin understand his daughter’s musical choice.

activities.prompt: What does Shruti want to do with fusion music?
options: Leave it untried.
Change it into one note.
Give it a fair try.
Use it only for asides.
activities.explanation: Shruti wants to give fusion music a fair try.

activities.prompt: Put Shruti’s early thoughts in the order she has them.
items: Shruti first thinks
of practising once
then of leaving the group
activities.explanation: She first thinks of practising once, and then thinks of leaving the group.

activities.prompt: Match each play-language term with its meaning.
pairs: A single sound at a particular pitch
activities.explanation: Asides address the audience. Fillers fill pauses, notes have pitch, and crescendo increases volume.

activities.prompt: Which set is fully supported by the lesson?
options: Shruti wants to leave; her family are painters; Nabin shows clear anger.
Shruti wants silence; her family are dancers; Nabin quietly hides his pride.
Shruti wants to criticise; her family are readers; Nabin claps very softly.
Shruti wants a fair try; her family are vocalists; Nabin shows pride.
activities.explanation: These details match Shruti’s choice, her musical family and Nabin’s proud response.

activities.prompt: Shruti plans to practise once, then leave. She wants to give fusion music a fair try. She does not know how to speak to her father properly. What does this suggest?
options: She has fully accepted it and knows exactly what to say.
She has decided to leave, so she refuses to test the music.
She wants to test the music, but she is not fully committed.
She dislikes fusion music and wants another kind instead.

why.She has fully accepted it and knows exac: This mistakes her cautious plan for complete confidence in staying.
why.She has decided to leave, so she refuses: This ignores her wish to give fusion music a fair try.
why.She dislikes fusion music and wants anot: This treats hesitation as a complete dislike of fusion music.

activities.explanation: This matches both her fair trial and her plan to leave.

activities.prompt: Nabin claps furiously and looks proud. He praises Shruti instead of criticising her. How does he probably feel?
options: He is ashamed of Shruti and unhappy with her singing.
He is proud of Shruti and pleased with her performance.
He is angry with Shruti but praises her to be polite.
He is proud of his own music but unhappy with Shruti’s.

why.He is ashamed of Shruti and unhappy with: Pride and praise do not support shame or unhappiness.
why.He is angry with Shruti but praises her: There is no sign that his praise hides anger.
why.He is proud of his own music but unhappy: His praise is for Shruti, not against his own music.

activities.explanation: His fierce clapping and praise show pride in Shruti.

activities.prompt: Shruti’s grandfather, father and uncles were all vocalists. What can we say about her family’s musical background?
options: The family has no interest in music or singing at all.
The family only respects loud music and dislikes quiet songs.
The family changed its musical tradition after Shruti was born.
The family has a strong musical tradition based on singing.

why.The family has no interest in music or s: This ignores that her close relatives were all vocalists.
why.The family only respects loud music and: Being vocalists does not mean the family likes only loud music.
why.The family changed its musical tradition: The facts do not say that the family changed its tradition.

activities.explanation: Several family members being vocalists show a musical family tradition.

activities.prompt: Leela helps Nabin understand his daughter’s musical choice. Nabin admits he had underestimated his own music. What has Leela helped him do?
options: She has helped him see Shruti’s choice more clearly.
She has helped him reject Shruti’s choice and music.
She has helped him blame Shruti for confusing his music.
She has helped him stop thinking about music altogether.

why.She has helped him reject Shruti’s choic: Understanding a choice does not mean deciding to reject it.
why.She has helped him blame Shruti for conf: Leela is helping him understand, not blame his daughter.
why.She has helped him stop thinking about m: Nothing in the facts says he wants to avoid the topic.

activities.explanation: This matches Leela’s stated help in understanding the choice.

activities.prompt: One character uses an aside to address the audience. Another uses a non-lexical filler to fill a pause. How do these choices differ?
options: The first fills silence; the second shares a thought.
The first changes the voice’s pitch; the second changes its volume.
The first shares a thought; the second fills silence.
The first hides all thoughts; the second removes every spoken word.

why.The first fills silence; the second shar: This reverses the purposes of an aside and a filler.
why.The first changes the voice’s pitch; the: Addressing the audience is not a pitch or volume change.
why.The first hides all thoughts; the second: An aside shares thoughts, while a filler does not remove words.

activities.explanation: An aside shares with the audience; a filler fills a pause.

activities.prompt: One note has a steady pitch in the melody. A crescendo makes the sound grow louder little by little. What happens to the note?
options: Its pitch rises steadily while its volume stays constant.
Its pitch stays steady while its volume gradually increases.
Its pitch and volume both change very quickly.
It becomes several notes with different pitches at once.

why.Its pitch rises steadily while its volum: Growing louder changes volume, not the note’s pitch.
why.Its pitch and volume both change very qu: The increase is gradual, not a quick change in both features.
why.It becomes several notes with different: A note remains one sound at one pitch, even when it grows louder.

activities.explanation: A crescendo increases volume gradually while the note keeps its pitch.

lessons.title: Drama Skills, Writing and Music

activities.prompt: How can a few words and sounds make a character’s feelings come alive?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Drama, Scripts and Music
activities.body: Drama can change the meaning and feeling of dialogue through stress and intonation. In a script, a colon introduces a speaker’s words, while brackets give instructions for acting. Shruti’s stressed words show internal conflict. Music offers another way to express ideas: Anuradha has learnt tabla since primary school, and her mother and brother support her ambition. Indigenous instruments use natural materials.
keyPoints: Stress and intonation can change dialogue.
A colon introduces a speaker’s words.
Brackets give acting instructions.
Anuradha’s family supports her musical ambition.
activities.explanation: Drama writing and music can all express strong feelings and ideas.

activities.prompt: Shruti must perform a line. How can her voice show her inner conflict?
steps: Stress “don’t” because it shows her wish to pull back.
Stress “do” because it shows her wish to act.
Let her voice rise at the end because it shows sincerity.
Use both because stress and intonation make her conflict clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which can change the meaning and emotional impact of dialogue?
options: Stress and intonation
Tabla and bamboo
A colon and brackets
Anuradha and Shruti
activities.explanation: Stress and intonation can change dialogue’s meaning and emotional impact.

activities.prompt: A colon introduces a speaker’s ______ in a script.
activities.hint: Think of the words spoken by the character.
activities.explanation: A colon shows when a speaker’s words begin.

activities.prompt: Match each drama clue with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each clue shows how scripts, voices and stressed words guide actors.

activities.prompt: Put the natural materials in the order they appear in your lesson.
items: bamboo
gourds
animal hides
activities.explanation: Your lesson lists bamboo, gourds and animal hides in this order.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Anuradha is true?
options: She has learnt tabla since primary school years.
Her father approves of her musical ambition.
Her mother and brother oppose her musical ambition.
She joins only performances her father approves of.
activities.explanation: Anuradha has learnt tabla since primary school, despite her father’s disapproval.

activities.prompt: Match each example with its detail from the lesson.
pairs: Has learnt tabla since primary school years
Was formed in 2012 and includes children
Features a silly king, nine ministers and a bed bug
activities.explanation: These pairs match each example with the detail given in your lesson.

activities.prompt: Shruti feels two opposite wishes inside. Which words should she stress?
options: She should stress “don’t” and “do”.
She should stress “I” and “want”.
She should stress “not” and “want”.
She should stress “her” and “conflict”.

This mistake focuses on herself and her wish.
This mistake focuses on negation instead of the two sides.
This mistake names the feeling instead of stressing key words.

activities.explanation: Stressing “don’t” and “do” shows her inner conflict.

activities.prompt: Shruti’s voice rises towards the end of her words. How may her tone sound?
options: She sounds calm and certain.
She sounds sincere and open.
She sounds cross and angry.
She sounds bored and tired.

The rising voice shows that Shruti is sincere.
This mistake assumes every rising voice shows anger.
This mistake treats a rising voice as tiredness, not sincerity.

activities.explanation: This mistake reads a rising voice as calmness, not sincerity.

activities.prompt: Two friends choose different music paths. What does “Each bay, its own wind” suggest?
options: Each friend has a unique path.
Each friend must follow one path.
Each friend needs the same path.
Each friend should avoid any path.

Music comforts the speaker during sadness.
Music helps her through difficult times.

Therefore, music helps her pull through hard times.

activities.prompt: How do Nabin’s concerns about performing too often and performing with an orchestra differ?

The first issue concerns how often Shruti should perform; the second concerns how the orchestra may affect her style. Although he has stated his views on fusion music several times, that does not make the concerns the same. Shruti must consider both the limit on performances and the effect of the orchestra.

lessons.title: Khetaram, the Desert Postman

activities.prompt: How does Khetaram keep families connected across the burning desert?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Khetaram
activities.body: Khetaram works as the Gramin Dak Sewak at Somarad Branch Post Office. He carries mail between the village and its families. He is its only postman and has served them for fifteen years. His left shoulder droops from carrying a mailbag. He crosses the harsh Thar desert beyond Barmer, the last railhead. He delivers mail at the border within twenty-four hours. Severe heat may delay deliveries until after sunset.
keyPoints: His work connects the village and its families.
His route crosses the harsh Thar desert.
Severe heat may delay deliveries until after sunset.
activities.explanation: This introduces Khetaram's work, route, and main challenge.

activities.prompt: Why might Khetaram deliver post after sunset instead of during the day?
steps: He crosses harsh desert heat, officially forty-nine point nine degrees Celsius.
He carries an official mailbag that cannot weigh more than twenty-eight kilos.
Delivering it can mean walking twenty kilometres for one delivery.
So he should wait until sunset when severe heat would stop him.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: At Somarad Branch Post Office, what is Khetaram?

The only postman
A shopkeeper
A bus driver

activities.explanation: Years of carrying the mailbag have made his left shoulder droop.

activities.explanation: The official limit is twenty-eight kilos, so the bag cannot be heavier.

activities.prompt: Match each detail about Khetaram with its correct fact.

activities.body: India Post reaches people across India, including distant settlements and hard-to-reach interior areas. Gramin Dak Sewaks provide the only link with distant settlements. activities.explanation: Each worker or system had a different role in postal delivery.

activities.prompt: Which fact best explains why GDS workers matter in interior areas?
options: Company dak did not travel between administrative centres.
GDS workers serve only administrative centres.
Other means cannot easily reach these interior areas.
Rural depositors keep their savings at home.
activities.explanation: GDS workers deliver in interior areas that other means cannot easily reach.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for receiving a letter in the right order.
items: Mail is dropped into a post box.
A postman delivers the mail.
The postman places it in the recipient's letter box.
activities.explanation: This was the mail delivery process described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which option correctly links India's wider reach with the trust shown by accounts?
options: Before independence, company dak reached everyone, and postal accounts show trust.
In 1947, India Post had 25,000 post offices, and delivery agents show trust.
After independence, Khetaram changed post offices, and postal accounts show reach.
After independence, India Post aimed to reach all, and accounts show trust.
activities.explanation: After independence, India Post aimed to reach the whole population. Operational accounts show people's trust.

activities.prompt: A girl in a distant settlement waits for a letter each week. What does she expect?
options: The Gramin Dak Sewak will carry the letter to her.
The nearest shop will carry the letter to her.
The office will send company dak to her home.
The letter will reach her without anyone carrying it.

why.The nearest shop will carry the letter t: This confuses a postal worker with an ordinary shop.
why.The office will send company dak to her: This wrongly treats old company dak as a home-delivery system.
why.The letter will reach her without anyone: This ignores that a postman must deliver the letter.

activities.explanation: This matches the GDS role as the link with distant settlements.

activities.prompt: A report says GDS workers enter interior areas. What does “interior areas” mean here?
options: far places inside a region
busy markets inside the main city
postal buildings inside a busy city
riverside places inside every region

why.busy markets inside the main city: This mistakes inland places for crowded city markets.
why.postal buildings inside a busy city: This confuses delivery areas with buildings used by offices.
why.riverside places inside every region: This limits inland areas to riverside places.

activities.explanation: This means difficult inner places, not busy city centres.

activities.prompt: GDS workers make up more than half the postal workforce. What does this show?
options: Distant deliveries depend greatly on GDS workers.
Most postal work happens inside busy city offices.
Only a few workers deliver mail to distant homes.
Company dak now carries most of India's mail.

why.Most postal work happens inside busy cit: It wrongly assumes most workers work in cities.
why.Only a few workers deliver mail to dista: It ignores that GDS workers are the distant link.
why.Company dak now carries most of India's: It mistakes the old company system for the present one.

activities.explanation: It combines the large GDS share with their distant-area role.

activities.prompt: In 1947, India had 25,000 post offices. Why did this help the new postal aim?
options: It helped bring the whole population within reach.
It returned mail to the old company system.
It made every distant home receive daily letters.
It reduced the need to reach the whole population.

why.It returned mail to the old company syst: Independence aimed to expand reach, not restore company control.
why.It made every distant home receive daily: Having offices does not promise daily delivery to every home.
why.It reduced the need to reach the whole p: More offices support reach, rather than reducing the need for it.

activities.explanation: Many offices supported the aim of reaching the whole population.

activities.prompt: A family keeps savings at a rural post office. What does this suggest about the family?
options: They trust the postal system with their savings.
They are forced to keep money at the post office.
They think only shops can hold savings.
They do not believe the postal system is useful.

why.They are forced to keep money at the pos: The facts describe a service, not a forced saving system.
This confuses rural post offices with ordinary shops.
why.They do not believe the postal system is: Using the service for savings shows belief in its usefulness.

activities.explanation: Keeping savings there suggests trust in the postal system.

lessons.title: Khetaram and His Village

activities.prompt: What did Khetaram discover about work, family, and hope?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A New Way to Earn
activities.body: Khetaram became a GDS worker, gaining another way to earn. This access is essential for GDS selection. He works five hours daily and earns a salary and steady income. His appointment gave him a new lease of life. One good crop of bajra cannot feed his family of five. They would starve without his job income. Many families partly depend on relatives’ money orders. The patwari replacement proposal was rejected.
keyPoints: Another way to earn is essential for GDS selection.
Khetaram’s salary gives his family steady income.
One good crop of bajra cannot feed his family of five.
activities.explanation: This card explains how Khetaram’s new job supports his family.

activities.prompt: Khetaram’s family has five people. One good bajra crop cannot feed them all. How can his job protect them from hunger?
steps: His job gives him a salary and steady income.
This help matters because one bajra crop cannot feed five people.
Without the job income, his family would starve.
So, the job is essential for his family’s survival.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does the Job Give?
activities.prompt: What do the GDS conditions give workers?
options: Five hours of daily work
A salary and steady income
News of death
A cell phone and the post
activities.explanation: The GDS conditions give workers both a salary and steady income.

activities.title: A Good Crop
activities.prompt: One crop of bajra in a good year can feed Khetaram’s family of five.
activities.explanation: The lesson says one good crop cannot feed his family of five.

activities.title: Without the Job Income
activities.prompt: Without the income from his job, Khetaram’s family would ______.
activities.hint: Think about what would happen if the family had no income.
activities.explanation: The family would starve without the income from Khetaram’s job.

activities.title: GDS Selection
activities.prompt: What is essential for GDS selection?
options: Access to another livelihood
Replacement by more patwaris
Rejection of daily work
Steady phone line access
activities.explanation: Access to another way to earn is essential for GDS selection.

activities.title: Phone Lines and the Post
activities.prompt: Phone lines may one day let Khetaram carry both a cell phone and the post.
activities.explanation: The lesson says phone lines may one day make this possible.

activities.title: Order by Book Page
activities.prompt: Put these lesson moments in book-page order.
items: His appointment gives him a new lease of life.
A torn envelope corner warns him of death.
Phone lines may let him carry a cell phone and the post.
activities.explanation: These details appear on pages 208, 209, and 210.

activities.prompt: Khetaram receives a steady salary from his five-hour GDS job. How does this appointment change his life and his family?
options: It gives his family hope and a steadier daily life.
It removes the need to grow any food for them.
It makes every relative stop sending money to the village.
It changes the village crop into a better and richer one.

why.It removes the need to grow any food for: This mistake thinks paid work makes food growing unnecessary.
why.It makes every relative stop sending mon: This mistake ignores the money orders that relatives still send.
why.It changes the village crop into a bette: This mistake thinks a job changes the quality of the crops.

activities.explanation: The salary and steady income give Khetaram a new lease of life.

activities.prompt: Khetaram’s job gives his family steady income. One good bajra crop cannot feed his family of five. If that income stopped, what would likely happen?
options: His family would starve because the crop is not enough.
His family would eat well because the year was good.
His family would need no help from money orders.
His family would grow more food from the same crop.

why.His family would eat well because the ye: A good year still cannot make one crop enough for five people.
why.His family would need no help from money: Money orders may still help, so the crop is not the only need.
why.His family would grow more food from the: His job income helps prevent the family from starving.

activities.explanation: Without another income source, the family would starve.

activities.prompt: A letter for Khetaram has a torn corner. He knows it may bring news of death. How might he feel?
options: He may feel deep worry about the person.
He may feel sure that everyone is safe.
He may feel excited about the good news.
He may feel bored because the letter is short.

A torn corner signals possible death, not sure safety.
The clue points to possible death, not good news.
why.He may feel bored because the letter is: The torn corner gives no reason to think the letter is short.

activities.explanation: News of death can make him fear something bad before reading.

activities.prompt: Many families depend partly on money orders sent by relatives. If these orders stopped, what might happen to some families?
options: Some families might lose part of their support.
Every family might lose all of their support.
No family might need any money support.
All families might grow much more food.

why.Every family might lose all of their sup: This mistake changes partly into only and loses the limit.
This mistake denies the support that money orders can provide.
This mistake wrongly connects lost money orders with more food.

activities.explanation: These families depend partly on the money that relatives send.

activities.prompt: GDS workers work five hours and receive a salary with steady income. A proposal to replace them with patwaris was rejected. What may explain this?
options: The workers offer an important livelihood with steady pay.
The workers can feed five people with one bajra crop.
The workers spend ten hours without receiving any salary.
The workers refuse to read letters or write replies.

why.The workers can feed five people with on: This mistake mixes up what one crop can feed with job income.
why.The workers spend ten hours without rece: This mistake changes five working hours into ten unpaid hours.
why.The workers refuse to read letters or wr: This mistake turns Khetaram’s reading and writing skill into a refusal.

activities.explanation: Their work gives an important livelihood with steady income, so it is valuable.

activities.prompt: Access to another means of livelihood is essential for GDS selection. What does “livelihood” mean in this fact?
options: A way to earn money for daily needs
A letter that carries news of death
A plan to replace GDS workers with patwaris
A five-hour duty without any steady pay

why.A letter that carries news of death: This mistake connects livelihood with the torn envelope.
why.A plan to replace GDS workers with patwa: This mistake connects livelihood with the rejected proposal.
why.A five-hour duty without any steady pay: This mistake connects livelihood with working hours, not earnings.

activities.explanation: A livelihood is a means of earning a living.
