lessons.title: Letters, Stamps and Telegrams

activities.prompt: Why did every word in a telegram matter so much?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Writing and postal memories
activities.body: A group discussion compared a postcard, inland letter, envelope and money order form. A condolence message expresses sorrow and offers strength to a grieving family. The Ministry of Culture created the Daakroom carnival to bring back letter writing. The study of postage stamps and postal history is called philately.
keyPoints: Different postal items were compared in a group discussion.
A condolence message offers strength to a grieving family.
Philately is the study of postage stamps and postal history.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects letter writing, condolence messages, stamps and telegrams.

activities.prompt: How should you write a quick telegram when every word affects its price?
steps: Telegram was formerly used for quick, short, and specific messages.
Leave out extra words because every word affects the price.
Use clear, exact words so the message stays short and specific.
The best telegram is brief, precise, and specific.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: More about letters and telegrams
activities.body: The Daakroom carnival also held competitions and workshops about writing and post. It aimed to provide a digital detox, meaning time away from digital use, and revive letter writing. India Post, the Ministry of Culture, Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti supported it. Telegram writers used short messages and had to make every word precise.
keyPoints: The carnival held writing and post competitions and workshops.
The carnival aimed to revive letter writing.
Telegram writers had to make every word precise.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how people promoted letter writing and used telegrams carefully.

activities.prompt: Which set was compared in a group discussion?
options: A postcard, telegram and stamp
A postcard, inland letter, envelope and money order form
A stamp, telegram and condolence message
An inland letter, carnival and post office
activities.explanation: The group discussion compared a postcard, inland letter, envelope and money order form.

activities.prompt: A telegram was formerly used for long, vague messages.
activities.explanation: Telegram writers used quick, short and specific messages.

activities.prompt: The study of postage stamps and postal history is called ______.
activities.hint: This word names the study of stamps and postal history.
activities.explanation: Philately means studying postage stamps and postal history.

activities.prompt: Why did telegram writers have to be precise?
options: Every word changed the message
Every word affected the price
Every word made the message longer
Every word showed the writer's age
activities.explanation: Telegram writers had to be precise because every word affected the price.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its meaning.
pairs: sorrow and strength for a grieving family
an event to bring back letter writing
the study of postage stamps and postal history
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an item with the meaning given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the telegram message qualities in the order used in the lesson.
items: quick
short
specific
activities.explanation: The lesson describes telegram messages as quick, short and specific.

activities.prompt: The Daakroom carnival has writing competitions, workshops, and support from several groups. A child writes more letters and takes a digital break. Why does this fit?
options: It aimed to collect stamps and study postal history.
It aimed to compare forms and choose a telegram.
It aimed to revive letter writing and give a digital detox.
It aimed to send condolences to grieving families.

why.It aimed to collect stamps and study pos: This mistake mixes the carnival with stamp study and postal history.
why.It aimed to compare forms and choose a t: This mistake treats the carnival as a form comparison activity.
why.It aimed to send condolences to grieving: This mistake mistakes a writing event for condolence message sending.

activities.explanation: It matches the aim to revive letters and provide a digital detox.

activities.prompt: One telegram writer uses extra words. Why might it cost more than another telegram?
options: Extra words can make the message more cheerful.
Extra words can make the message less specific.
Extra words can change the writer's postal history.
Every extra word can increase the price.

why.Extra words can make the message more ch: This mistake thinks extra words change the writer's mood.
why.Extra words can make the message less sp: This mistake confuses price with the message's clarity.
why.Extra words can change the writer's post: This mistake connects telegram wording with stamp history.

activities.explanation: This is right because every word affects the telegram's price.

lessons.title: The Value of Words

activities.prompt: What makes a few simple words feel truly precious?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words and the Heart
activities.body: The poem begins with a doubt: words may not satisfy the heart. Words can leave it caring for more. The poet compares words to summer birds that fly away. Only empty air is left behind. Yet a few truthful words may bring deeper joy. A voice with few words can also cheer a lonely home. Such words are precious.
keyPoints: Words may not satisfy the heart.
Few truthful words can bring deeper joy.
A voice with few words can cheer a lonely home.
activities.explanation: The poem shows that the worth of words depends on what they give.

activities.prompt: Your friend is sad. One person gives a long talk. Another says only two kind words. Who helps more?
steps: A long talk may miss the heart, because many words feel empty.
A few true words can bring deep joy, because they feel real.
Few kind words can cheer a lonely home, because they are precious.
So two kind words help more, because true words beat many.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: More Words Are Not Always Better
activities.body: The poem shows that more words do not always mean more value. Words can seem as worthless as weeds when the heart needs them. A few truthful words may bring deeper joy than many words. The poem also imagines that satisfying the chest would let the world hold a feast. Flowering plants may look grand but fail to produce fruit. This image also shows why grand words may not help.
keyPoints: Words can be worthless when the heart needs them.
A few truthful words may bring deeper joy.
Grand-looking words may fail to help.
activities.explanation: The poem values useful, truthful words more than a large number of empty words.

activities.prompt: The poet compares words to which things?
options: Flowering plants
Summer birds
Lonely homes
Summer weeds
activities.explanation: The poet compares words to summer birds that fly away.

activities.prompt: A few truthful words can bring deeper ______ than many words.
activities.hint: This is a strong feeling of happiness.
activities.explanation: The poem says that a few truthful words can bring deeper joy.

activities.prompt: Match each image or group to what the poem says about it.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an image and the effect connected with it in the poem.

activities.prompt: A voice with few words cheers a lonely home. How does the poem value those words?
options: They are noisy.
They are ordinary.
They are precious.
They are empty.
activities.explanation: The few words spoken by such a voice are very precious.

activities.prompt: Put the poet's comparison in order.
items: Words are compared to summer birds.
The summer birds fly away.
Only empty air is left behind.
activities.explanation: The comparison moves from words to birds, their flight, and what remains.

activities.prompt: A speaker's words look grand, but they do not produce real help. Which image fits best?
options: Flowering plants that bear no fruit.
Summer birds that fly away.
A feast prepared for the world.
A voice with few words.
activities.explanation: Flowering plants may look grand but fail to produce fruit, like words that do not help.

activities.prompt: Ravi's friend makes many big promises. This week, none of them happen. Ravi thinks of summer birds flying off. What does Ravi feel is left?
options: only empty air, because the words did not stay
a warm heart, because the words were many
a full feast, because the words sounded grand
deep joy, because the friend spoke well

why.a warm heart, because the words were man: Wrong: many words do not make the heart warm here.
why.a full feast, because the words sounded: Wrong: a feast comes from a full heart, not grand words.
why.deep joy, because the friend spoke well: Wrong: joy comes from true words, not many words.

activities.explanation: Right: the birds leave empty air, so the promises leave nothing.

activities.prompt: Nina feels very sad. She needs kind words today. Her friend talks and talks, but says nothing kind. Nina thinks the words are like weeds. Why does she feel this?
options: the words are useless, because her heart needs kindness now
the words are pretty, because her friend talks a lot
the words are rare, because her friend is often quiet
the words are strong, because her friend speaks loudly

why.the words are pretty, because her friend: Wrong: many words are not pretty when they give no comfort.
why.the words are rare, because her friend i: Wrong: the friend is talking, so the words are not rare.
why.the words are strong, because her friend: Wrong: loud words can still be worthless like weeds.

activities.explanation: Right: weeds are worthless when the heart needs help.

activities.prompt: Ben gets a long, noisy card from a shop. His sister writes him one short, true line. The short line makes Ben happier. Why is he happier?
options: a few true words can bring deeper joy, than many empty words
a long card is always better, because it costs more
his sister wrote less, so she did not care much
shop cards are bad, because they are not made at home

why.a long card is always better, because it: Wrong: this forgets that many words can feel empty.
why.his sister wrote less, so she did not ca: Wrong: few words can be precious, not careless.
why.shop cards are bad, because they are not: Wrong: home or shop does not decide the joy.

activities.explanation: Right: the poem says few truthful words bring deeper joy.

activities.prompt: A garden plant has big, bright flowers. It looks grand to everyone. But by autumn it has no fruit. A speaker uses big, fancy words but gives no help. What does the plant show about the words?
options: grand words may look fine but give no real fruit
big flowers always mean the plant is useful
fancy words are better because they sound grand
the plant failed because nobody watered it

why.big flowers always mean the plant is use: Wrong: the flowers look fine but still give no fruit.
why.fancy words are better because they soun: Wrong: sounding grand does not make words helpful.
why.the plant failed because nobody watered: Wrong: water is not part of what the plant shows here.

activities.explanation: Right: grand plants can fail to give fruit, like grand words.

activities.prompt: A mother listens as her son finally shares his worry. Her heart now feels full and calm. She says the whole world could hold a feast. What does she mean?
options: her full heart brings wide joy, like a big feast
she wants to cook food for the whole world
her son must plan a real party for her
her heart is empty, so she needs a feast

why.she wants to cook food for the whole wor: Wrong: the feast is a picture of joy, not real cooking.
why.her son must plan a real party for her: Wrong: she is speaking of her heart, not a real party.
why.her heart is empty, so she needs a feast: Wrong: her heart feels full, not empty.

activities.explanation: Right: a full chest is imagined as a feast for the world.

lessons.title: Poetry, Communication and Expression

activities.prompt: How can a few words change how someone feels?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Poetry and Words Express Ideas
activities.body: Poetry makes ideas vivid through comparisons. A simile compares words with birds. A metaphor describes the heart as a pilgrim. Another comparison places words among worthless weeds. Hyperbole exaggerates, like a world holding a feast. Metre has one stressed and one unstressed syllable. The poem Weigh Your Words urges careful speech. Students make an emoji to show an expression. Charles-Michel de l’Épée is called the father of sign language.
keyPoints: Poetry uses simile, metaphor and hyperbole.
Metre has one stressed and one unstressed syllable.
Idle words can cause pain in a heart.
activities.explanation: You will see how poetry works and why careful words matter.

activities.prompt: Your friend is angry and wants to say a mean word fast. Should he say it?
steps: An angry word can hurt someone's heart, so a quick word is risky.
That hurt can stay, so it is hard to erase later.
Weighing each sentence first helps, because you can choose a kind word.
So speak only what you truly mean, and avoid idle words.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the Simile
activities.prompt: Which image compares words with birds?
options: The pilgrim-heart image
The summer-bird image
The world-feast image
The weed-words image
activities.explanation: The summer-bird phrase compares words with birds, so it is a simile.

activities.title: Complete the Metre
activities.prompt: A metre has a stressed and an ______ syllable.
activities.hint: This syllable receives less stress.
activities.explanation: A metre consists of one stressed and one unstressed syllable.

activities.title: Match Images and Patterns
activities.prompt: Match each image or pattern with its name.
activities.explanation: The summer-bird image is a simile. The pilgrim-heart image is a metaphor, and the feast is hyperbole. The syllable pair shows metre.

activities.title: Words Without Impact
activities.prompt: What happens when words depart and leave empty air?
options: They make no impact.
They change the metre.
They become hyperbole.
They show an expression.
activities.explanation: The lesson says such words make no impact. The poem therefore urges careful speech.

activities.title: Put the Images in Page Order
activities.prompt: Put these images in their page order in your book.
items: The summer-bird comparison
The world-feast image
The emoji expression game
Weigh Your Words
activities.explanation: They come from pages 221, 222, 229 and 230, in that order.

activities.title: Weigh Your Words
activities.prompt: Why should each sentence be weighed carefully?
options: Metres need one stressed syllable.
Feasts need more word guests.
Words can hurt and last.
Signs need clear faces.
activities.explanation: The poem says an idle word can cause pain. Words may leave an impact that is hard to erase.

activities.prompt: Ravi's friend called him a bad name. Ravi still feels sad after one week. Why does Ravi still feel sad?
options: The words left a mark hard to erase.
Ravi has forgotten the words already.
Ravi feels sad because his friend said sorry.
Ravi feels sad because he said the bad name.

This wrongly thinks forgetting is why Ravi feels sad.
why.Ravi feels sad because his friend said s: This wrongly thinks an apology causes the hurt.
why.Ravi feels sad because he said the bad n: This mixes up who said the bad name.

activities.explanation: Right: the words left a mark that is hard to erase.

activities.prompt: Sam makes a quick joke without thinking. His friend starts to cry. What does the poem warn about an idle word?
options: It can bring pain to a heart.
It is always funny and kind.
It is a word that is very true.
It can never reach a person.

This wrongly thinks an idle word is always harmless.
This wrongly thinks idle means true and sincere.
This wrongly thinks idle words never reach anyone.

activities.explanation: Right: an idle word can bring pain to a heart.

activities.prompt: Mia wants to reply fast to a rude message. Her teacher says, 'Weigh each sentence.' What should Mia do?
options: Think about each sentence before she speaks.
Send the first words that come to mind.
Use long words so people will listen.
Stop talking to her friend forever and ever.

This wrongly thinks quick words are the best words.
This wrongly thinks long words show more care.
why.Stop talking to her friend forever and e: This wrongly takes the advice much too far.

activities.explanation: Right: weighing a sentence means thinking before speaking.

activities.context: On a severe-heat day at Somarad Branch Post Office, Khetaram prepares to cross the Thar desert with an official mailbag. He is the only postman there and has served the village and its families as a trusted link for fifteen years. Years of carrying the mailbag have left his left shoulder drooping. His route begins beyond the last railhead at Barmer, and some deliveries may require a twenty-kilometre walk. The recorded temperature is forty-nine point nine degrees Celsius.
activities.prompt: Severe heat forces Khetaram to consider postponing a delivery until after sunset. What should he do next?
options: Wait for the heat to ease and then complete the delivery later.
Begin the longest walk immediately and finish before sunset.
Ask a second postman to take over the route.
Carry extra mail in a second bag so that he can finish sooner.

why.Begin the longest walk immediately and f: The facts do not say that he should continue walking in severe heat.
why.Ask a second postman to take over the ro: He is the only postman at Somarad Branch Post Office.
why.Carry extra mail in a second bag so that: Adding another bag could take the mail beyond the official weight limit.

activities.explanation: Severe heat can force him to delay deliveries until after sunset.

activities.context: On a severe-heat day at Somarad Branch Post Office, Khetaram prepares to cross the Thar desert with an official mailbag. He is the only postman there and has served the village and its families as a trusted link for fifteen years. Years of carrying the mailbag have left his left shoulder drooping. His route begins beyond the last railhead at Barmer, and some deliveries may require a twenty-kilometre walk. The recorded temperature is forty-nine point nine degrees Celsius.
activities.prompt: Waiting until after sunset may threaten the border delivery within twenty-four hours of dispatch. What should Khetaram consider?
options: Balance the possible heat-related delay against the twenty-four-hour delivery target.
Ignore the delivery target completely and delay every delivery.
Deliver in the severe heat immediately and add mail to finish sooner.
Transfer the entire route to another postman without checking the target.

why.Ignore the delivery target completely an: He must still consider reaching the border within twenty-four hours of dispatch.
why.Deliver in the severe heat immediately a: Severe heat may require a delay, while adding mail could exceed the weight limit.
why.Transfer the entire route to another pos: There is no other postman at Somarad Branch Post Office.

activities.explanation: Both the possible delay and the delivery target matter.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Khetaram's left shoulder droops because years of carrying the mailbag have affected it.
Reason (R): Repeatedly carrying the official mailbag has made his left shoulder droop.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and repeated carrying explains the condition of his shoulder.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Khetaram could depend on another postman at Somarad Branch Post Office to help during severe heat.
Reason (R): Severe heat sometimes forces him to delay deliveries until after sunset.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because he is the only postman there, although the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why Khetaram's work can affect both his body and the timing of his deliveries.
activities.answer: Khetaram's work affects his body because years of carrying a mailbag have made his left shoulder droop. It also affects the timing and effort of each round. He crosses the harsh Thar desert on a route beginning beyond the last railhead at Barmer, and he may walk twenty kilometres for one delivery. His official mailbag cannot exceed twenty-eight kilos. Since he is the only postman at Somarad Branch Post Office, the responsibility for reaching village families also rests on him, while severe heat can force him to delay deliveries until after sunset.
points: Years of carrying the mailbag have affected his shoulder.
His route crosses the harsh Thar desert beyond Barmer.
A single delivery may involve a twenty-kilometre walk.
Severe heat and the need to be the only postman affect delivery timing.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Before 2001, Khetaram worked as a delivery agent. After India accepted more than three lakh delivery agents as Gramin Dak Sewaks, he joined this workforce, which now forms more than half of the total workforce. In Ladakh, Lakshadweep and the riverine communities of the north-east, GDS workers reach interior areas that other means cannot easily reach. A letter dropped into a post box is finally placed by a postman in the recipient’s letter box.
activities.prompt: If GDS workers could no longer serve distant settlements, what would likely happen to mail sent there?
options: It might remain undelivered because no other means can easily reach the affected places.
It would be delivered through company dak between administrative centres.
It would reach only administrative centres and not remote households.
It would be delivered more quickly because postmen already handle final delivery.

why.It would be delivered through company da: Company dak served administrative centres, not distant settlements.
why.It would reach only administrative centr: Administrative centres are not substitutes for remote delivery.
why.It would be delivered more quickly becau: The postman’s final step cannot replace the missing delivery network.

activities.explanation: Removing GDS workers breaks the link with remote places.

activities.context: Before 2001, Khetaram worked as a delivery agent. After India accepted more than three lakh delivery agents as Gramin Dak Sewaks, he joined this workforce, which now forms more than half of the total workforce. In Ladakh, Lakshadweep and the riverine communities of the north-east, GDS workers reach interior areas that other means cannot easily reach. A letter dropped into a post box is finally placed by a postman in the recipient’s letter box.
activities.prompt: Khetaram now works in which role, and why is this role suitable for remote settlements?
options: He is a Gramin Dak Sewak, since this workforce is vital for reaching far-off places.
He remains a delivery agent under the British system, since company dak served every settlement.
He manages post offices, since there were 25,000 of them in 1947.
He handles postal savings, since rural depositors are the main users of the service.

why.He remains a delivery agent under the Br: Company dak did not serve every remote settlement.
why.He manages post offices, since there wer: The post-office figure does not describe his work in the case.
why.He handles postal savings, since rural d: Postal savings and delivery work are separate roles.

activities.explanation: Khetaram became part of the GDS workforce.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Gramin Dak Sewaks are the only link with distant settlements.
Reason (R): They deliver in interior areas that other means cannot easily reach.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Their ability to reach difficult interior areas explains why they are the only link with distant settlements.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Khetaram was called a delivery agent before 2001.
Reason (R): Gramin Dak Sewaks make up more than half of the total workforce.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The size of the GDS workforce does not explain Khetaram’s earlier designation as a delivery agent.

activities.prompt: Explain how Gramin Dak Sewaks expand the reach of India Post and why their role matters in remote areas.
activities.answer: Gramin Dak Sewaks make India Post’s reach possible in places where other means cannot easily travel. They serve as the only link with distant settlements, and their work covers interior areas in Ladakh, Lakshadweep and the riverine communities of the north-east. This role became part of a large workforce: India accepted more than three lakh delivery agents as GDS, and these workers form more than half of the total workforce. Thus, they connect remote communities with the postal system and help fulfil the aim of bringing the whole population within reach.
points: GDS workers are the only link with distant settlements.
They deliver in interior areas that other means cannot easily reach.
They serve GDS territories such as Ladakh and Lakshadweep.
They form more than half of the total workforce.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Khetaram was selected as a Gramin Dak Sewak and works five hours a day. This job gives him a salary and steady income. His family has five members, and one bajra crop in a good year cannot feed them all. The family would starve without his wages. Khetaram reads letters and writes replies for people. A torn corner on an envelope tells him that the letter carries news of death. Families partly survive through money orders sent by relatives.
activities.prompt: If Khetaram's GDS job suddenly ended, what would be the most likely result for his family?
options: They would lose the income that helps prevent them from going hungry.
They would have enough to eat because one good bajra harvest is sufficient.
They would certainly remain safe because relatives' money orders would replace the missing wages.
They would be better off because the job takes only five hours each day.

why.They would have enough to eat because on: One good bajra harvest cannot feed all five family members.
why.They would certainly remain safe because: Money orders support many families only partly and cannot be assumed to replace the wages.
why.They would be better off because the job: Shorter working hours do not mean that losing the income would improve the family's situation.

activities.explanation: The job provides the steady income his family needs to survive.

activities.context: Khetaram was selected as a Gramin Dak Sewak and works five hours a day. This job gives him a salary and steady income. His family has five members, and one bajra crop in a good year cannot feed them all. The family would starve without his wages. Khetaram reads letters and writes replies for people. A torn corner on an envelope tells him that the letter carries news of death. Families partly survive through money orders sent by relatives.
activities.prompt: If phone lines become available and Khetaram can carry both a cell phone and the post, what would this make possible?
options: He could deal with phone messages while continuing to handle postal work.
He would have to abandon postal work once he began using the phone.
He could stop doing GDS work because calls would provide his entire income.
He could use phone calls instead of reading and writing letters for everyone.

why.He would have to abandon postal work onc: The new development would not require him to give up postal work.
why.He could stop doing GDS work because cal: Phone calls would not necessarily replace his GDS income.
why.He could use phone calls instead of read: The possibility of carrying a phone does not mean that letter services would end.

activities.explanation: The two forms of communication could be carried and used together.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Khetaram's family would starve without the income from his GDS job.
Reason (R): His GDS job gives him a salary and a steady income.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The steady income from the job explains why the family could not survive without it.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A Gramin Dak Sewak must work only five hours each day.
Reason (R): GDS workers must spend the whole day on duty.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the stated reason contradicts the five-hour working condition.

activities.prompt: Explain how Khetaram's GDS appointment changes his family's situation.
activities.answer: Khetaram's appointment gives him a new lease of life because it creates a source of regular pay. His wages provide a steady income to a family of five that cannot be fed by one bajra crop even in a good year. Without this income, the family would starve. His work also uses his ability to read letters and write replies for people. Money orders from relatives support many families partly, while his own employment gives his household a dependable means of survival.
points: His appointment gives him a new lease of life.
The job provides a salary and steady income.
One bajra crop cannot feed his family of five even in a good year.
His family would starve without the income from his job.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Ministry of Culture created the Daakroom carnival.
Reason (R): The carnival aimed to provide a digital detox and revive letter writing.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The stated aims provide a possible reason for creating the carnival.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A person must own stamps before studying philately.
Reason (R): Philately is the study of postage stamps and postal history, and a person can study stamps without owning any.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason shows that studying stamps does not require owning them.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a condolence message and a telegram?
activities.answer: A condolence message is written for a grieving family. It shows sorrow about the family's loss and gives them strength. A telegram, by contrast, was formerly used to send a quick, short and specific message. Its writer had to choose words carefully because every word affected the price. Thus, the main difference is their purpose and style: a condolence supports a family in grief, while a telegram delivers brief, precise information.
points: A condolence message expresses sorrow.
A condolence message offers strength to a grieving family.
A telegram was formerly used for quick, short and specific messages.
Telegram writers had to be precise because every word affected the price.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Follow That Dream
chapters.summary: In this chapter: a dream begins with passion; following a dream through obstacles; critical thinking and language; talking, writing and inspired goals.

lessons.title: A Dream Begins with Passion

activities.prompt: What turns an interest into a dream strong enough to guide your choices?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Journey Towards a Dream
activities.body: A true dream keeps a person awake and does not appear only in sleep. Great people have a dream and work towards it. The journey begins with passion for a particular interest. Belief comes next, and the dreamer counts effort, money and sacrifice. Reaching a world-class standard needs focused, intense work for about ten years. The thought of success keeps a dreamer going when energy is low.
keyPoints: True dreams stay with you during waking hours.
Effort and sacrifice help turn dreams into achievements.
Dreams can belong to sports, science, arts, business or design.
activities.explanation: These ideas show what a dreamer needs from passion to achievement.

activities.prompt: How should a science dream grow?
steps: The student loves science because passion starts every dream journey.
The student believes the dream must be realised because passion causes belief.
The student counts years, money, and sacrifices because the dream has costs.
The student accepts about ten focused years because the road is difficult.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A True Dream
activities.prompt: What does a true dream do to a person?
options: Keeps them awake
Appears only in sleep
Makes them stop working
Makes every task easy
activities.explanation: A true dream stays with you while you are awake.

activities.title: Years of Focused Work
activities.prompt: Reaching a world-class standard needs focused and intense work for about ______ years.
activities.hint: Think about the long effort described.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives about ten years of focused, intense work.

activities.title: Great People and Their Dreams
activities.prompt: Great people become great because they have a dream and work towards it.
activities.explanation: Great people have a dream and work towards it.

activities.title: Join the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each beginning to its ending.
pairs: have a dream and work towards it
that the dream must be realised
must count the years of effort, money and sacrifice
activities.explanation: Belief, careful counting and focused work all support the dream.

activities.title: The Dreamer's Path
activities.prompt: Put the steps towards a dream in the correct order.
items: Feel passion for a particular interest
Believe that the dream must be realised
Count the years of effort, money and sacrifice
Work with focused intensity for about ten years
activities.explanation: The lesson presents passion, belief, counting and hard work as a path.

activities.title: Keeping the Dream Alive
activities.prompt: Which plan best supports a dreamer when the road is difficult?
options: Count the needs and keep going when energy is low
Ignore effort and wait for easy success
Count only money and avoid all sacrifice
Stop when the work becomes difficult
activities.explanation: The dreamer counts effort, money and sacrifice. The thought of success keeps them going.

activities.prompt: A poem says, "My dream walks beside me all day." What does the line imply about the speaker?
options: The speaker's dream lives beyond sleep.
The speaker's dream appears only in sleep.
The speaker is afraid to sleep each night.
The speaker has already reached great success.

why.The speaker's dream appears only in slee: This wrongly treats dreams as things that appear only during sleep.
why.The speaker is afraid to sleep each nigh: This wrongly connects a living dream with fear of sleeping.
why.The speaker has already reached great su: This wrongly treats a dream as proof that success has already happened.

activities.explanation: A true dream stays with a person even during waking hours.

activities.prompt: The painter enjoys making posters. She now believes her art dream must be realised. What came first in her journey?
options: Her passion for making posters came first.
Her strong belief in success came first.
Her years of hard sacrifice came first.
Her world-class painting skill came first.

This reverses the order by putting belief before passion.
This mistakes a later sacrifice for the beginning of the journey.
why.Her world-class painting skill came firs: This mistakes an outcome for the passion that begins the journey.

activities.explanation: Passion starts the journey, and strong belief comes afterwards.

activities.prompt: The student counts the years, money, and sacrifice needed. This happens before training for a science dream. What does this show about the student's dream?
options: She knows that reaching her dream has costs.
She expects her science dream to be easy.
She believes success will come without work.
She wants her teacher to choose the dream.

why.She expects her science dream to be easy: This wrongly assumes that a worthy dream will be easy.
why.She believes success will come without w: This wrongly assumes that success does not need work.
why.She wants her teacher to choose the drea: This wrongly thinks that the teacher, not the dreamer, chooses the dream.

activities.explanation: Counting these things shows awareness of the dream's costs.

activities.prompt: The dancer wants world-class skill but tries only easy practice. What must change in the dancer's plan?
options: He needs focused, intense work for about ten years.
He needs more sleep instead of steady practice.
He needs a different dream without hard effort.
He needs to choose between dream and passion.

why.He needs more sleep instead of steady pr: This wrongly believes rest can replace the effort needed for skill.
why.He needs a different dream without hard: This wrongly treats changing dreams as a way to avoid work.
why.He needs to choose between dream and pas: This wrongly believes passion and a dream must be separated.

activities.explanation: World-class skill needs about ten years of focused, intense work.

activities.prompt: The runner feels tired after a hard match. She thinks about success and keeps training. Why does she continue?
options: The thought of success gives her strength.
Winning removes every hard part from training.
Her tired feeling proves her dream is weak.
Other people order her to keep training.

why.Winning removes every hard part from tra: This wrongly believes winning makes training easy.
why.Her tired feeling proves her dream is we: This wrongly treats tiredness as proof that a dream is weak.
This wrongly believes the runner continues only because of orders.

activities.explanation: Thinking about success can give energy when the runner feels low.

activities.prompt: The designer dreams of creating a new product. The designer thinks success will make the road easy. What should the designer understand about the road?
options: The road will likely stay difficult for most of the journey.
The road will become easy after the first day.
The dream will remove the need for any effort.
The dream will need no effort or sacrifice.

why.The road will become easy after the firs: This wrongly assumes difficulty ends after the first day.
why.The dream will remove the need for any e: This wrongly assumes a dream removes the effort needed.
why.The dream will need no effort or sacrifi: This wrongly assumes a dream needs no sacrifice.

activities.explanation: The lesson says the road may remain difficult for most of the journey.

lessons.title: Following a Dream Through Obstacles

activities.prompt: What helps a dream survive when life changes the path?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Dreams Need Support and Sacrifice
activities.body: Many people never move beyond wishful thinking, so their dreams stay dreams. Some may choose security instead of pursuing a dream. Unexpected circumstances or life itself may change a person's direction and dreams. A changed dream can take longer to realise. People who stand by you can offer support. Turning an aspiration into reality needs significant effort and personal sacrifices.
keyPoints: Support comes from people who stood by a successful person.
Unexpected events can change a person's direction and dreams.
Realising a dream needs significant effort and personal sacrifices.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects following dreams with support, changing plans, effort and personal sacrifices.

activities.prompt: A student has a dream and supports siblings. What should they do?
steps: First, support the siblings through school, because they need help.
Next, accept that life may change the dream.
Unexpected circumstances can change life's direction.
Finally, make effort and sacrifices, because they turn dreams into reality.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Dreams or Reality?
activities.prompt: Some dreamers never move beyond wishful thinking.
activities.explanation: Some dreamers never move beyond wishful thinking. Their dreams may remain only dreams.

activities.title: The Mother's Advice
activities.prompt: The mother tells her daughter to ignore the time needed for her dream.
activities.explanation: The mother encourages her daughter. She also warns her to consider the time needed to chase the dream.

activities.title: Leaving School for Work
activities.prompt: Why did some people leave school for work?
options: To help their friends change direction
To keep their own dreams unchanged
To encourage their mother to worry
To support their siblings through school
activities.explanation: Some people left school for work so they could support their siblings through school. Good choice!

activities.title: Choices and Changes
activities.prompt: Match each beginning with what the lesson says.
pairs: They choose it instead of pursuing a dream
Some people leave school for work
They can support their siblings through school
She warns about the time needed
They can change a person's life direction
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a choice or event with its result from the lesson.

activities.title: When Life Changes a Dream
activities.prompt: After life changes a person's dream, what may happen next?
options: It may become wishful thinking again
It must stay exactly the same
It may take longer to realise
It will be realised without effort
activities.explanation: A changed dream may take longer to realise. Turning an aspiration into reality also needs significant effort.

activities.title: Thanking a Support Network
activities.prompt: Which people do award winners usually thank?
options: Strangers who never gave support
The people who stood by them
People who only watched their success
People who chose dreams for them
activities.explanation: Award winners usually thank the people who formed their support network. These are the people who stood by them.

activities.prompt: An award winner thanks the friends who supported her. Why?
options: She knows they formed her support network.
They stopped her from reaching success.
They expected her to give up her dream.
She thinks her award alone explains her success.

This mistake turns support into a barrier to success.
This mistake treats encouragement as pressure to quit.
why.She thinks her award alone explains her: This mistake ignores the support network behind successful people.

activities.explanation: This is right because successful people have people who stood by them.

activities.prompt: A boy talks about dreams but never acts. What does this show?
options: He stays inside wishful thinking alone.
He already has a strong support network.
He has fully realised his dream already.
He has chosen security over his dream.

This mistake assumes that talking about dreams shows support.
This mistake treats talking about a dream as achieving it.
This mistake assumes an unstated choice instead of wishful thinking.

activities.explanation: This is right because some dreamers never move beyond wishful thinking.

lessons.title: Critical Thinking and Language

activities.prompt: What helps a dream survive when the journey gets difficult?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Thinking About Your Dreams
activities.body: Dreams can change as life changes. This does not mean giving up. It means your dream may evolve and gain new participants. Commitment means making a complete commitment to an activity. A realistic view of effort, investment and sacrifice can prevent early abandonment. The path may feel like a maze of hurdles, but achievers continue until their dreams become true.
keyPoints: Dreams can evolve and gain new participants.
Commitment means making a complete commitment to an activity.
Realistic assessment can prevent early abandonment.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you think carefully about change, effort and persistence.

activities.prompt: Ming fears changing a dream means giving up. What should she think?
steps: Dreams can change with life, so Ming need not keep the first one.
Reviewing effort, investment and sacrifice helps prevent early abandonment.
A plunge means full commitment, so achievers continue until dreams become true.
Therefore, Ming should assess the change and commit to her changed dream.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In “dreamscape”, what does the part “-scape” mean?
options: A path or hurdle
A view or scene
A dream that changes
A complete commitment
activities.explanation: The part “-scape” means a view or scene.

activities.prompt: The first conditional is used for real or possible situations in the ______.
activities.hint: Choose the time word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The first conditional describes real or possible situations in the future.

activities.prompt: Why does the mother encourage Ming while also showing some caution?
options: She wants Ming to avoid every kind of hurdle.
She wants Ming to choose a completely different dream.
She wants Ming to consider the years involved.
She wants Ming to leave the journey behind.
activities.explanation: The mother supports Ming but asks Ming to consider the years involved.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of experiential learning in the order given in the lesson.
items: experience
action
reflection
activities.explanation: The lesson gives the order as experience, action and reflection.

activities.prompt: A person's dream changes, and more people become participants. What does this show?
options: The dream must stay fixed for ever.
The dream can evolve as life changes.
The journey must end without action.
New participants must reject the changed dream.
activities.explanation: Dreams can evolve with life, and more people may join a changed dream.

activities.prompt: Ming faces many hurdles while working towards a dream. What does an achiever do?
options: Continue until the dream becomes true
Stop when the first hurdle appears
Change the dream at every hurdle
Wait for someone else to pursue it
activities.explanation: A dream's path has hurdles. Achievers keep pursuing it until it becomes true.

activities.prompt: Ming changes her dream and reviews her effort and sacrifice. She then shares the changed dream with other people. What may happen?
options: The changed dream must be kept away from other people.
More people may become participants in her changed dream.
Her old effort becomes worthless whenever the dream changes.
Her changed dream must stop as soon as others join it.

why.The changed dream must be kept away from: It mistakes support for a reason to keep the dream private.
why.Her old effort becomes worthless wheneve: It believes any change makes earlier effort and sacrifice worthless.
why.Her changed dream must stop as soon as o: It mistakes joining by others for a reason to stop pursuing the dream.

activities.explanation: A changed dream can gain more participants when other people join.

activities.prompt: A child makes a complete plunge and keeps pursuing the dream. What does this show about the child's approach?
options: It shows casual interest without serious pursuit of the dream.
It shows full commitment but early abandonment of the dream.
It shows a wish to change the dream before real effort.
It shows full commitment and steady pursuit of the dream.

why.It shows casual interest without serious: It mistakes trying for a while for making a complete commitment.
why.It shows full commitment but early aband: It treats commitment as a reason to abandon the dream early.
why.It shows a wish to change the dream befo: It mistakes changing interests for maintaining full commitment.

activities.explanation: A plunge means full commitment, and achievers continue pursuing their dreams.

activities.prompt: A child tries a task, watches it, and reflects on the result. What kind of learning is this?
options: It is learning through experience, action and reflection.
It is learning by reading rules without trying the task.
It is learning by watching others without trying anything.
It is learning by guessing results without checking them properly.

why.It is learning by reading rules without: It confuses reading with the experience and reflection shown here.
why.It is learning by watching others withou: It confuses watching others with personal experience and action.
why.It is learning by guessing results witho: It confuses guessing with checking what happened through action.

activities.explanation: The child acts, experiences the task, and reflects on the result.

activities.prompt: The mother reminds Ming that years are involved but remains hopeful. How should her words be understood?
options: She believes every careful dream will fail after many years.
She wants Ming to reject any dream that asks for effort.
She feels certain the dream will succeed without any effort.
She balances encouragement with careful thought about the years.

why.She believes every careful dream will fa: It mistakes caution about time for belief that dreams must fail.
why.She wants Ming to reject any dream that: It mistakes a request for careful thought as a wish to abandon effort.
why.She feels certain the dream will succeed: It mistakes hope for certainty that effort and sacrifice are unnecessary.

activities.explanation: Her hopeful tone supports Ming while asking her to consider the years.

lessons.title: Talking, Writing and Inspired Goals

activities.prompt: What steps could help your dream grow into something real?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Messages, Dreams and Goals
activities.body: The lesson brings together talking, writing and goal setting. A listening announcement shares news about vocational courses starting at school. Applicants can choose a course, while different people give advice about dreams and planning. Email sends and receives electronic messages. A vision board shows goals, dreams and inspirations. It helps you focus and stay motivated. Stories from the Ramayana and Mahabharata shaped Shivaji's leadership ideals and bravery.
keyPoints: Vocational courses will start at school, and applicants can choose a course.
Roles offer advice about dreams, planning and backup plans.
Email carries electronic messages, while a vision board supports goals and motivation.
Stories shaped Shivaji's leadership ideals and bravery.
activities.explanation: These are the lesson's main ideas about messages, dreams and goals.

activities.prompt: A student wants a vocational course at school. The student has no plan or backup. What should they do?
steps: Check the announcement because the courses start in school.
Choose a course because applicants are given a choice.
Make a plan because dreams need planning.
Prepare a backup because the friend will ask about it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the listening announcement about?
options: Vocational courses starting at school
An email for sending messages
A vision board for showing goals
A dream that needs planning
activities.explanation: The announcement shares news about vocational courses starting at school.

activities.prompt: Match each role with its advice.
pairs: Says a dream can always be pursued later
Reminds the dreamer that dreams need planning
Asks the dreamer about a backup plan
activities.explanation: The parent, mentor and friend each give different advice.

activities.prompt: What is a vision board?
options: An email for electronic messages
A visual guide to your goals
A choice of school course
A planning reminder for dreamers
activities.explanation: A vision board visually represents a person's goals, dreams and inspirations.

activities.prompt: What did Jijabai instil in Shivaji?
options: Planning, courses and classes
Patriotism, justice and dharma
Messages, goals and dreams
Desires, classes and emails
activities.explanation: Jijabai instilled a strong sense of dharma, patriotism and justice in Shivaji.

activities.prompt: The stories from the Ramayana and ______ shaped Shivaji's leadership ideals and bravery.
activities.hint: Choose the other story named with the Ramayana.
activities.explanation: Both story collections shaped Shivaji's leadership ideals and bravery.

activities.prompt: Put the course announcement steps in order.
items: Announce vocational courses starting at school
Give applicants a choice of course
Conduct vocational classes at school
activities.explanation: The announcement comes first, applicants choose a course, and classes are conducted at school.

activities.prompt: The school announcement says vocational courses will start in school. Applicants can choose a course. How might an applicant feel?
options: They may feel excited because they can choose one.
They may feel upset because they must choose one.
They may feel bored because the courses start at school.
They may feel afraid because every choice is fixed.

why.They may feel upset because they must ch: This mistakes the applicant's choice for a fixed choice.
why.They may feel bored because the courses: Starting courses at school does not explain feeling bored.
why.They may feel afraid because every choic: Choosing one course does not mean every choice is fixed.

activities.explanation: Choosing a course can make an applicant feel excited.

activities.prompt: The mentor says that dreams need planning. A student has chosen a vocational course. What should the student do next?
options: Make a plan for reaching the chosen course.
Start the course without making any plan.
Ask the school to choose a different course.
Wait until later because the dream can wait.

why.Start the course without making any plan: This ignores the mentor's warning that dreams need planning.
why.Ask the school to choose a different cou: This reverses the applicant's choice and still misses planning.
why.Wait until later because the dream can w: This follows the parent's idea but ignores the need for planning.

activities.explanation: Planning is needed before working toward the chosen course.

activities.prompt: The friend asks the dreamer about a backup plan. Why does the friend ask?
options: To help the dreamer prepare if the first plan fails.
To stop the dreamer from choosing any school course.
To make the dreamer forget their main dream.
To prove that every dream must end very soon.

why.To stop the dreamer from choosing any sc: This wrongly says the friend wants no course chosen.
why.To make the dreamer forget their main dr: This wrongly suggests the friend wants the main dream forgotten.
why.To prove that every dream must end very: This invents a rule that every dream must end very soon.

activities.explanation: A backup plan helps the dreamer prepare for another possible path.

activities.prompt: A vision board shows a person's goals, dreams and inspirations. It helps a person focus and stay motivated. A student feels distracted while working. What should the student do?
options: Use the board to refocus and stay motivated.
Remove the board because goals may cause distraction.
Add many wishes to the board without choosing one goal.
Wait for new motivation without looking at the board.

why.Remove the board because goals may cause: This wrongly says goals and dreams cause distraction.
why.Add many wishes to the board without cho: This adds more wishes instead of focusing on one goal.
why.Wait for new motivation without looking: This ignores the board's help for staying motivated.

activities.explanation: The board helps the student focus and stay motivated.

activities.prompt: Jijabai instilled dharma, patriotism and justice in Shivaji. Stories shaped his leadership ideals and bravery. Queen Madalasa taught her children to understand the soul and avoid material desires. What do these influences do?
options: They guide people towards strong values and wise actions.
They help people gain more material desires.
They teach people to ignore their duties and values.
They turn every good influence into a material wish.

why.They help people gain more material desi: This reverses Queen Madalasa's teaching about material desires.
why.They teach people to ignore their duties: This reverses the values taught by Jijabai and the stories.
why.They turn every good influence into a ma: This confuses good influences with wanting material things.

activities.explanation: All three influences encourage values that guide wise actions.

lessons.title: Believe in Yourself and Face Change

activities.prompt: What could help you take the first step toward a brighter future?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Facing Your Future
activities.body: The poem encourages you to face change and difficult choices. It shows fear pushing you backwards and comfort stopping your growth. Staying in comfort may feel easy, but taking the first step is hardest. Self-belief can keep your future on the right track. The speaker understands your struggle, guides you, and speaks directly to you.
keyPoints: Change is a personal journey involving the future.
Comfort can stop people from growing.
Self-belief can guide your future.
activities.explanation: This poem gives you courage to face change and believe in yourself.

activities.prompt: Mia always sits with the same friends at lunch. A new girl invites her to the art club. Mia feels scared. Should she stay where it is easy or try the club?
steps: Mia feels safe with her old friends, so staying there is the easy choice.
But staying only with them means she will not meet new people, so comfort stops her growth.
Her fear makes her want to step back, but fear can push a person backwards.
If she believes in herself and takes the hard first step, her future can stay on track, so she should try the club.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Poem’s Voice and Mood
activities.body: The poem begins in a thoughtful mood and ends with determination. Its overall tone is motivational and encouraging. The speaker understands your struggle and acts like a guide. The capitalised word ‘You’ creates a close connection. The first step is an image for the difficulty of starting a new challenge or change.
keyPoints: The poem moves from thoughtfulness to determination.
The speaker understands your struggle.
The first step shows how difficult beginning can be.
activities.explanation: The poem speaks warmly to you and helps you feel ready for change.

activities.title: A Personal Journey
activities.prompt: What does the poem present the challenge as?
options: A comfortable return to the past
A personal journey involving the future
A carefree holiday
A simple game with friends
activities.explanation: The challenge becomes a personal journey that involves your future.

activities.prompt: The poem says that staying in comfort is easy.
activities.explanation: The poem presents comfort as easy, even though it can stop growth.

activities.prompt: The poem shows that fear can push a person ______.
activities.hint: Think about the direction fear can make you move.
activities.explanation: Fear can hold you back, but self-belief can help you move forward.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea to what the poem says about it.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how comfort, fear, and self-belief affect your journey.

activities.title: How the Tone Changes
activities.prompt: How does the poem’s tone change from beginning to end?
options: From happiness to complete silence
From calmness to uncertainty
From thoughtfulness to determination
From confusion to sadness
activities.explanation: The opening is thoughtful, while the ending gives readers determination.

activities.title: Remember the First Step
activities.prompt: You face a new challenge. What should you remember about its first step?
options: It is the hardest part of beginning.
It is the easiest part of beginning.
It is a reason to avoid beginning.
It is unrelated to a new challenge.
activities.explanation: Beginning feels difficult, but believing in yourself can keep your future on track.

activities.prompt: Sam plays the same easy game every day. He never tries new games. He begins to feel bored and stuck. What does comfort do to Sam here?
options: It stops him from growing.
It makes him feel brave and ready.
It pushes him backwards with fear.
It makes his choices hard to make.

This confuses comfort with courage, but comfort is easy, not brave.
This mixes comfort with fear, which is a different idea.
This mixes comfort with hard choices, which come with change.

activities.explanation: Correct: comfort keeps Sam stuck, so he does not grow.

activities.prompt: A girl wants to join the school play. She is afraid to walk on stage the first time. Her friend says, "Just take the first step." What does the friend mean?
options: The start is the hardest part, so begin anyway.
She should wait until she feels no fear.
She should stay off the stage for now.
The whole play will be easy after today.

This mistakes the first step for waiting until fear is gone.
This mistakes the first step for giving up and staying back.
This mistakes a hard start for an easy whole play.

activities.explanation: Correct: the first step is hardest, so she must start.

activities.prompt: A boy has a hard test coming. He thinks, "I always fail." His teacher says, "Believe in yourself." He studies and does well. What did self-belief do for him?
options: It kept his future on the right track.
It made the test easy with no work.
It stopped him from feeling any fear.
It kept him safe in his comfort zone.

This thinks belief replaces hard work, but he still studied.
This thinks belief removes all fear, but fear can still come.
This confuses self-belief with staying comfortable.

activities.explanation: Correct: self-belief keeps his future on the right track.

activities.prompt: A girl practised her speech many times. On the day, fear filled her mind. She went back to her seat without speaking. What did fear do to her?
options: It pushed her backwards from her goal.
It helped her speak with more courage.
It made her take her first step.
It kept her future on the right track.

This confuses fear with courage, but she did not speak.
This thinks fear helps action, but she stepped back.
This confuses fear with self-belief, which moves forward.

activities.explanation: Correct: fear pushed her backwards from speaking.

lessons.title: Challenges, Courage and Role Models

activities.prompt: What helps us keep moving forward when life gets really hard?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Facing Difficult Beginnings
activities.body: Taking a first step is a metaphor for the difficult beginning of personal growth. Overcoming obstacles may need factors besides self-belief. The poem tells you to believe in yourself and hold on to courage. The last advice is to keep your hands and heart open. Ambedkar faced humiliations and discrimination. Lal Bahadur Shastri walked barefoot to attend school. Kalam's newspaper work taught him the value of hard work.
keyPoints: The first step represents a difficult beginning.
The poem advises self-belief, courage, and open hands and heart.
Role models show courage through difficult experiences.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects difficult beginnings, obstacles, self-belief, courage, and role models.

activities.prompt: Your friend calls learning to swim 'a steep first step'. He wants to quit after one hard lesson.
steps: The first lesson feels hard, so wanting to stop makes sense.
A hard first step is normal, so quitting now is too soon.
Self-belief alone may not be enough, so he also needs help.
A hard start is not the end; he should try with help.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the first step represent?
options: A hard beginning of personal growth
A quiet change of season
A slow end of growing up
A simple school journey
activities.explanation: The first step represents the difficult beginning of personal growth.

activities.prompt: A rhetorical ______ makes the reader think instead of requiring a direct answer.
activities.hint: Think of a question that needs no direct answer.
activities.explanation: A rhetorical question makes you think instead of requiring a direct answer.

activities.prompt: What happened to Ambedkar at school?
options: He faced humiliations and discrimination.
He left school and never returned.
He became a newspaper delivery boy.
He enjoyed an easy school journey.
activities.explanation: Ambedkar suffered humiliations and discrimination at school but did not give up.

activities.prompt: Match each person or idea to its lesson detail.
pairs: the present situation when things remain unchanged
a question that makes the reader think
worked as a newspaper delivery boy early in the morning
walked several miles barefoot to attend school in extreme weather
suffered humiliations and discrimination at school but did not give up
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a lesson idea with its correct detail.

activities.prompt: What does the lesson say about overcoming obstacles?
options: Only self-belief can overcome them.
Obstacles always disappear by themselves.
Factors besides self-belief may be needed.
Personal growth ends when obstacles appear.
activities.explanation: Overcoming obstacles may need factors besides self-belief.

activities.prompt: What was Ambedkar's role in the Drafting Committee of the Constitution of India?
options: Committee chairperson
Newspaper editor
School headteacher
Delivery guide
activities.explanation: Ambedkar later became Chairperson of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution of India.

activities.prompt: A girl calls the first day at school 'a steep hill'. She feels nervous but goes anyway. What does her metaphor most likely mean?
options: The first day feels very hard to start.
The school is built on a real hill.
She hates walking up all hills.
The first day will be short and easy.

This takes the metaphor as a real hill.
This mistakes one hard start for a hate of hills.
This ignores her nervous feeling and the hard start.

activities.explanation: Right: the metaphor shows a difficult beginning.

activities.prompt: A boy believes he can win the race. His old shoes are a daily obstacle. What is the best next step?
options: He should get better shoes and keep training.
He should just believe harder in himself.
He should stop running because shoes decide all.
He should hide his hurt feet from everyone.

why.He should just believe harder in himself: This wrongly says self-belief alone is enough.
why.He should stop running because shoes dec: This wrongly says one obstacle decides everything.
why.He should hide his hurt feet from everyo: This hides the problem instead of solving it.

activities.explanation: Right: belief helps, but he also needs a real fix.

activities.prompt: A girl asks, 'Do we want to waste our free hour?' Nobody answers her. What is she most likely doing?
options: She uses a rhetorical question to make them think.
She waits for a real answer from the class.
She forgets what she wanted to ask them.
She wants everyone to count the free hours.

why.She waits for a real answer from the cla: This treats a rhetorical question as a real one.
This guesses forgetting, but she asks clearly.
why.She wants everyone to count the free hou: This misreads the question as counting hours.

activities.explanation: Right: the question makes listeners think, not answer.

activities.prompt: A girl is treated unfairly at school but keeps studying. Later, she helps make fair rules for everyone. Why is she a role model?
options: She did not give up and later helped others.
She stopped studying after the unfair treatment.
She became perfect without any hard struggle.
She only wanted to become famous one day.

why.She stopped studying after the unfair tr: This ignores that she kept studying anyway.
why.She became perfect without any hard stru: This wrongly says she never had to struggle.
why.She only wanted to become famous one day: This gives a false reason and misses her help.

activities.explanation: Right: she faced unfair treatment but kept going.

activities.prompt: A boy fails a test and feels like quitting. He tells himself, 'Believe in yourself and hold on to courage.' Then he asks a friend for help and shares his notes. What does the poem most likely teach him?
options: Keep courage and keep your hands and heart open.
Hide your feelings and always work alone.
Give up when the first hard test comes.
Believe in yourself and never ask for help.

why.Hide your feelings and always work alone: This is the opposite of an open heart.
This ignores the poem's call to hold on.
why.Believe in yourself and never ask for he: This keeps belief but wrongly rejects help.

activities.explanation: Right: the poem advises courage and open hands.
